They wore not so active in the cause of educa-

But why this unwonted

activity? Let us see what the deputation said:
"Firmly convinced," they said, "of the

are anxious that no legislation should weaken

ment see in these Acts no question, but a con-
sideration of disease. They were ready
enough to see another question when we pro-
posed to protect little girls better. They were
ready enough in that case to see that (as they
fancied) such legislation would lead to evils.
They did not forget the indirect effect of such
legislation as that. But in the ease of these
Acts, what we have said from the beginning,
and to which they have turned a deaf ear, is
that you must look beyond the immediate
object of these Acts, and take into ac-
count their indirect effects. What we, who
oppose these Acts have all along said is, "this
system of legalized and regulated harlotry
increases the very cause of all the evil. It
increases the unrestrained passions of men."
What is a young man, we say, to think, who
nters into a town to find clean harlots pro-
vided for him by Government money? What
except that fornication is the natural thing

for him to turn to ? Increase the cause, we .1
say, and you stimulate the effect, and prosti-
tution must increase and flourish under these
Acts, because they are Acts which tend to .
increase fornicators.
These Members of Parliament are con-
tinually careless about giving any legal pro-
tection to a female child against seduction,
while they passionately desire and obstinately
fight for legal protection to men in committing
fornication. What a strange contrast is here!
Their apathy and opposition on the one hand,
their eager earnestness on the other!
When we have said that these laws are
immoral, a strange sort of answer has recently
been tramped up by their supporters. They
have come forward with a number of statistics
as to prostitutes who are reclaimed by the
Acts. In the deputation to Mr. BRUCE, to
which I have referred, this was especially
dwelt upon, and the deputation con-
gratulated one another on the moral
effects of the Acts. We know something of
what these " Reclamations" of women mean,
and how some women are "reclaimed under
the Acts a dozen times over! " But whtit I wish
to draw your attention to is that the state-
ment of the reclamation of prostitutes is no
answer to the argument that the Acts are
immoral; because the great question is,
" What is the effect of the Acts on Men ?"

; evidence of this, and also that men from a

indignant at prostitutes should be indig-
nant at these Acts ; and no wonder

maintained, their indignation should :turn

contend for a system which gives Government
sanction to such impurity, and makes elaborate
provision for carrying it on. The supporters

ife. Such a man robs his wife of everything

dealt with.

favour of these Acts—is like many other such
assertions, a lie, which has its origin in a long
tradition it AMC. It is always the way that
those who practice an abuse, or usurp a
privilege after they have possessed it a suffi-
cient time, come to regard its possession as an
unalterable law of nature. Hence it is that
classes of persons dare to tell us that the
, existence of prostitution is a law of nature.
There have boen many such lies which have
been held out to be laws of nature. Slave
owners argued for slavery that it was a law
of nature, and that the world would be
destroyed if slavery was broken down. So it
is with the land question—our great lauded
proprietors think and act as if the existencs
of large private estates must continue till the
world come to an ena. So it is with the con-
test between capital and labour; one would think
when one hears a capitalist argue, that the
existence of the laws of GOD were dependent
on the existence of large capitalists. Depend
upon it, Sir, it will be so till the end of the
world, that those who practice an abuse will
maintain that it is necessary that they should
do so.

AN excellent instance has just occurred
again illustrating the one-sided character of
the numbers of the present House of Com-
mons. Your readers are aware that at present,
if a man seduce a girl who is upwards of
twelve years of age, he can plead as excuse

establish that, he cannot be punished. In the
eyes of the law, a little girl of twelve years
old, though a mere child, is regarded, for the
purposes of seduction, as being a woman of
mature age, Our best criminal Judges have
commented over and over again on the injus-
tiee of this law, but perhaps the best comment
on it is to be found in the records of the
Rescue Society, which show the large numbers

baying been seduced at that age, and for whom

again it has been urged on Parliament that a

This has been espeCially urged on the present
Parliament, but a deaf ear has been
turned to the question. At present there

ago from twelve to fourteen, yet I am

chance for its passing—nobody is interested

that, it generally meets with opposition, and

that if you increase the punishment inflicted

more encouragement to woman falsely to
accuse men, and you will increase the danger

THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACTS.

IT is not my wont to reply to personal
attacks, but I beg you, on this oat:lesion, to
allow me to say a few words on the subject of
a clause in Mr. HUMPHREY SANDWITH'S letter in
your paper of May 11th. My few words are not
addressed to Mr. SANDWITH, with whom I have
no desire to argue the point, but they are
intended for the working men and women
who read your paper. Sentiments of justice
and of compassion still live and burn strongly
in the breasts of working men, as 1 know by
experience. I do not think it likely that they
would believe that we who have taken up the
cause of the down-trodden of our own sex,
could ever have been guilty of the cruelty
which Mr. S.isnwrrH imputes to us; never-
theless, I turn to them, without fear of being
accused by them of egotism, to tell them a
few facts Which may be an added assurance of

the sincerity of those who have identified
themselves with the poor outcast, in order to

deliver her from sin and. woe.

Mr. SANDIVITIeS accusation runs, as fol-
lows :—" Ladies who formerly treated frail
Women as something worse than the beasts
whie,h perish, who spurned them with
contumely, who 'gathered up the skirts of their
robes as they passed to save themselves. from
the touch of pollution, who, in fine, when a
poor sister fell, did their utmost to thrust her
down yet deeper in the mire," &c. Now, Sir, let
ma state a few facts. For years before our pre-

sent agitation began, we (ladies who are now
coming forward to purify the laws relating to
this question) were accustomed to relieve the
oppression of our own hearts in regard to this
subject, by helping individually every outcast
woman whom we could lay hands on. We
have not been content with merely aiding by

contributions of money the various rescue
agencies; we have gone forth, by night as
well as by day, into the streets and corners of
our cities to speak lovingly to the fallen. We
have sought them in prisons, in lock hospitals,
in wotkhouses, yes, even in brothels ; and
not by rebukes or preachings, but by tender
human sympathy, we have drawn numbers
from these places to our own homes, and back
into the paths of virtue. Sir, can Mr. SAND-
IVITIE say he has done as much? I know
that when I speak (driven by traducers to
speak, though reluctantly) of what I myself
have 'done, I am only recording what other
ladies have also done with yet greater devo-
tion. I have, Sir, but one little spare bedroom
in my house, not being a " grand lady."
Into that little room I have received, with my
husband's joyful consent, one after another of
these my fellow sisters; we have given to
then in the hour of trouble, sickness, and
death, the best that our house could afford,
and requested friends of a higher rank who
visited us to go to a neighbouring hotel. In
that little room I have nursed poor outcasts
filled with disease, and have loved them as if
they were my own sisters. Many have died in
my arms. We afterwards hired a little house,
and called it the "House of Rest," into which
we received others who came. Not far from us
there is a cemetery, in a sunny corner of which
there stands a row of humble graves, beneath
whieh lie the earthly remains of these our
" children," " fallen women," "prostitutes,"
if you like to call them so, but now resting in
the bosom of that SATIOUR who came to "seek
and to save that which was lost." For every
one of these departed in good hope, and joy-
fullyehaving found, besides the deeper peace,
the treasure of a pure friendship before they

died.
Sir, Mr. SANDWITII and other gentlemen
would do well to be aware of the fact that we
ladies are not ignorant of this class; no, nor
yet of the secret lives of the "gentlemen" who
patronise this class. It is not only the lowest
'and poorest to whom we have joyfully
ministered of our best;: but we have received
into ourhouses,and tried to restore again to hope
and to society many a cast-off mistress of men
of fashion, and many despairing mother of a
bastard child, ignored and forsakenby its father.
So far, Sir, from our desiring to see sin
punished, we have all along declared our
earnest desire to sea every hospital (not special
hospitals only) thrown open for the reception
of sinful men and women suffering from this
blight of sin. So deep a compassion do I feel
(and I express the feeling of all true women)
for those who are visited by this sore judg-
ment, that I have sought out, not only women,
but the most miserable of men suffering from
ahumiliating disease—poor sailors, Norwegians,
Spaniards, Greeks, &e., who arrive in this
great seaport—and have laboured to convey to
them, in any language possible, the sense of
the possibility of a renewed moral life, and of
a higher manhood than. they had yet realised.
No loathsome attribute of this disease has
kept me and other ladies away fr, m this
labour of love—a labour of love deeply apy e-
elated by these afflicted. men and wont( n, who
quickly distinguish between the merely-pro res.
sional and the human interest taken n th 31a.
Sir, I am ashamed to be driven to this self- le-
fence, but I am still more ashamed Slat any
English gentleman should huve forced an
English lady to put forth such defence, or to

record what wo would rather for ever conceal,
seeing that we have only done what it was our
duty to- do for the poor and sinful.
JOSEPHINE E. BUTLER.

PLF,A. FOR WIDOWS AND SPINSTERS.
MANY personshesides Mr. JAIIIIB TRORNTON
flosfuNs, of the Reform Club, appear to labour
under the strange and unaccountable delusion
that the promoters of the " Women's Disabi-
lities Bill" do not consider married women
qualified or entitled to exercise the franchise.
Hr. HOSKINS therefore proceeds to pour forth
in your columns copious streams of gushing
rhetoric with the intent of showing that wives
are not a whit inferior to their unmated and
widowed sisters. One of his arguments is
quite worth quoting as a curiosity--"Mothers,'‘
he tells us, "undergo the pains and perils of
childbirth." Can any one be so unfeeling as to
forbid them the franchise after that? As, not-
withstanding reflected explanations, the posi-
tion of the promoters of this Bill is constantly
misunderstood, may I be permitted once
more to attempt, without being very sanguine
of success, in a few words. to clear up this
artificial mystery.
• I understood Mr. JACOB BRIGIIT and his
associates, without expressing either approval
or disapproval of the present eleotoral qualifi-
cation which entitles men to vote for members
of Parliament, but accepting it as an existing
fact, to desire only that women should be
placed in precisely the , same position—no
better, no worse—than men now occupy. In
fact, to administer the existing law of house-
hold suffrage irrespective of sex. This is
exactly the result that Mr. Joint STUART
MILL desired by his proposed amendment on
the late Reform Bill, for the word "men"
to substitute "persons." On the other hand,.
Mr. HOSKINi3, and others in the some fog, wish
that women should possess a privilege, or as
probably he would prefer to style it, to exercise
a right now denied to men.
I am a partner, let me say, in the dis-
tinguished house of Bosu, BUNCOMBE and Co.,
occupying, as everybody knows, extensive pre-
mises in Blarney-lane, city of London. All
the members of the firm reside on the premises,
so, according to the present law, despite our
recognised moral and intellectual qualifica-
tions, we are all disfranchised. By registering
the offices in one of the porter's names, this
would entitle him to vote, but the others would
still remain non-electors. Take another case,
which has really come off in the Registration
Court. A man lives with his brother, paying
him a stipulated sum for board and lodgings;
he does not occupy exclusively any particular
apartment, but has the run of the whole house
the result is, according to the present law, that
he is disqualified to exercise the franchise.
The same thing happens when a young man
lives at home. When two young men share
apartments, whatever rent they pay, neither
can claim a vote.
Such, then, being the present state of the
electoral law as affects joint occupancy of man
with man, is it at present either prudent or
judicious to claim that a preferenne should be
given when the joint occupant is a woman?
When this Bill has become law, sex will have
()eased to be a- political disability any more
than race or colour, and men and wornenwill be
plead on a platform of political equality. It
will then be quite time enough to consider the
case of those, both male and female, who may be
disfranchised by reason of joint occupancy,
and the claim of all such to vote shall have my
sympathy and support. It will no doubt be
an anomaly that widow and spinster electors
should lose their votes by becoming wives,
but the answer is, not that this is just, but that
men now acting similarly, labour undcr the
same disadvantage.
Just as those Tories who blindly oppose
every Reform are really the abettors of revo-
lution, so those unreasonable Radicals are
unwittingly the obstructors of progress who
refuse to accept Of partial improvements, and
whose cry is "all or nothing." Much of the
marvellous success of this question of
"Woman's Suffrage" is owing to the happy
results of the reforms already effected.
At the late School Board election many
were quite staggered to find that women
could quietly go to the poll to record their

votes; and it was not a little humiliating to
see that all those terrible erects they were
quite prepared to expect should follow, were
only the outpourings of a disordered imagina-
tion. The modest behaviour and remarkably
sensible advice of the two lady members of
the London School Board have justified many
in entertaining the possibility of soon seeing
a few such members of the :National Parlia-
ment.

When Mr. JACOB Bninnes Bill passes,

there is every reason to hope that the new
electors will so exercise their newly-acquired
rights of citizenship, as even to convince Mr.
BUMMED-HOPE of the error of his ways;
and if this may be fairly expected from house-
holding viidelis and spinsters, whom Mt
BOUVERIE politely styles "the leavings of
humanity," is it at all likely that the superior
section Of the feminiiiiiivorld—those wives.atul
mothers who, .:,uceoTding to Mr. HOSKINS,
undergo the pains and perils of childbirth"
—shall havo long, to wait before their right .to
vote is univdAnlly recognised?
B. D. MACKENZIE.

To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE. ,
Sul,—As direct imputations on my cha-
racter have been made by the Railway Service
Gazette, I venture to ask you to allow the fol-
lowing letter, addressed to that paper, to
appear in your columns.—l am, yours obe
diently, BAXTER LANGLEY.

To the Editor of the Railway Service Gazette.
IN reference to your leading article of last
week, I claim the privilege of fair play to
reply. Unfortunately the issue raised between
us is one of fact, and one of us must be in
error; but if you are, proven to be wrong, not
only is the basis of your argument removed,
but the argument founded thereon is erroneous,
and the strictures and imputations are deprived
of their justification.
The two special points are-
1. Did I, on or about the 17th April, send
you a letter for insertion in the Railway Ser-
vice Gazette of the following Saturday, and
did you suppress that letter? •
2. Did I thrust myself upon the meeting of
railway servants held at Montpelier Tavern,
Walworth-road, as described in the article
referred to?
The former of these is by far the more hn-
portantoind I should. pass over the latter if it
did not strengthen my allegations with refer-
ence to the former.
1. With reference to the letter which I state
was suppressed
The letter was written at my office in office
hours, and as it was unusual for me to write
anything of the kind during those hours, the
fad that I was writing an official letter to the
Railway Service Gazette was known to my
daughter and my clerks, all of whom distinctly
remember the fact.
Very few communications being sent by
post from this office, it is distinctly within the
memory of my junior clerk that he delivered
the letter in question at Fullwood's rents.
He also distinctly remembers bringing a
message back to the effect that Mr. kGreen-
wood would write to me thereon. In a short
time afterwards I received a note signed
"James Greenwood," referring to the:contents
of the letter in question. That gentleman
must, therefore, have received it.
The letter itself was written at the request
of the Executive Council, and was not a private
letter from me; it embodied the proposed
programme of the delegate meeting, which
programme contained some alterations which
had appeared. in no other copy of that docu-
ment. I assert that the identical programme
so amended was published as a separate docu-
ment by the editor of the Railway Service
Gazette, on Saturday the 27th, my letter (of
which that programme was a part) having
been suppressed in your publication of Satur-
day, the 20th, that is the week before. It
seems, clear, therefore, from the evidence in
your own columns, that you had received the
letter which I assert I sent to you on April
17th.
2. Now as to the second point—namely, my
conduct at the Montpelier. I should have
known nothing of the meeting had I not been
invited by ROM of the London and Brighton
men to attend. I can give their names if
required. On entering the room I was
was asked to take the chair, but declined on
the ground that I thought a railwiiy man
ought to preside. Two other gentlemen wore
proposed, but both declined ; and it was only
when no other person was found willing, I
reluctantly agreed to preside, because I did
not know exactly what was proposed to be
done at that meeting. I can name at least
six men who can testify to the accuracy of
this statement, but I have no doubt that
gfixty could be found who remember the facts.
You, Sir, were not present in the inedtiug, but
invited me to meet you afterwards, and you
said nothing in disparagement of my conduct
,on the occasion. -Every man at that meeting
know,: that you were in error in the statement
contained in your article on this point.
If with these facts before me, and a sense of
the injustice done to me and the London men
by the suppression of my letter, I have on
more than one occasion since spoke in strong
terms of your assertions, I think there is
some excuse, but I should sincerely regret any
expressions I may have used, and: should be
ready to withdraw them, if by so doing I
could hope to prevent further misunderstand-
ings, and could secure cordial co-operation in
the future. I shall be glad to learn that your
stAcmcnt,;—directly challenging my- veracity
—were written under a mistake, and that we
cart work together in the cause I have had so
long at heart. J, BAXTEIt' LISULDY.

being able to say that trade still continuos good;
and we might go a litth further, and say that the
present issue is the most favourable report the
society has put forth for more than 20 years, all
things considered. And this is saying a great
deal; but though we feel highly delighted at our
position and prospects, just allow the word of
caution. Let us appreciate our opportunities, and
guard our privileges; far, depend upon it, a reac-
tion will set in, and we may be palled to pass again
through troubloas times. Lot us, therefore, use
well what we can now obtain by the labour of our
hands, and when adversity comes we shall be
prepared. These thoughts spring from what we
see around us everywhere. Every article of pro-
duction is augmenting in price, a fact which will
hinder the toiler from being any better by the
raising of his wages or the shortening of his hours ;
and these additions in the price of the produce and
manufactures of labour will, no doubt, in a short
time, cause a reaction. Capital seems determined
to realise the lion's share of the profits of the
combination of talent, energy, and industry. The
problem between labour and capital is not yet
solved; and when it is solved effectually, capital
will have to be content with a smaller share of the
profits than it has heretofore enjoyed ; but until
that time arrives, it will be our duty as labourers
to peacefully, though firmly, take all the care we
can of both our time and our wages, and to more
clearly show our brother members what we mean,
and what we] consider to be the key to the
problem.

MILLINERS' TRADES UNION.

On Saturday a meeting of milliners and dross- ,
makers was held at the Institute, 43, Groat Port-
land-street, to form a trades union and benefit
society. The attendance was good, and great
interest was displayed by those present in the
movement. The circular convening the meeting
stated that "no one but young ladies will be
admitted ; " and consequently only four gentlemen,
including the secretary (Mr. Bradberry), were
allowed by special favour to witness the proceed-
ings. Miss Emily Faithfull occupied the chair.
The secretary road the rules, and said there
were 1,600 milliners in the Directory who were
proprietors who probably on an average employed
five "hands each in their establishments. These
people could make as much as £72,000 a year by
two hours per day overwork from their assistants,
and this amount would pay numerous 40s. flues if
the Act of Parliament was infringed. .
Miss Emily Faithfull said it was impossible for
any man or woman to be indifferent to the hard-
ships which milliners and dressmakers had endured.
Since Tom Hood wrote "The Song of the Shirt"
much sympathy had been expressed for those who
earned their subsistence by needlework, but
sympathy had not boon productive of much good.
Her own attention
.had been attracted to the
subject of the long hours of milliners nine years
ago, when an association was formed of ladies for
giving dressmakers more time to execute orders,
to enforce the employment of extra hands when
busy, and to put an end to long hours. For some
time this association went on well and did much
to stop Sunday work, but in a little while the
'employers refused to be dictated to. The remedy
really was in the workers' hands; but singly the
" workers dare not refuse unfair labour, because they
'were not in a position to demand any change.
Combination would give them the power they
needed. Fourteen hours a day was sheer cruelty.
A combination of workers would really protect the
employers, and the customers would learn to
have greater patience. She believed many em-
ployers Would be very glad to escape the necessity
of putting-so grievance a burden upon their fellow.
creatures. They had met together for a good

THE SEAMEN OF TILE PORT OF LONDON.
The seamen struck for an advance in the rate of
wages a few days ago, which has been conceded
by some of the large shipowners, but refused II
the smaller ones, and on Saturday afternoon abor
1,000 seamen formed at the east end of London in
procession, and, headed by a brass band, marched
past the offices of such of the shipowners as bad
granted the advance, giving three ringing cheers
outside each, after which they proceeded to the
Surrey side of the water to enlist the sympathY
and co-operation of the seamen who had lately
arrived. On their return, their numbers having
been somewhat increased, they held a meeting at
the Albion Tavern, Rateliff-highway, for the
purpose of forming themselves into a protection
society.

LANCASHIRE.

THE COTTON TRADE.
On Saturday afternoon, a meeting of delegates
of the East Lancashire Power-loom Weavers
Association was held at Accrington, when there
were 90 deputies present from Darwen, Church,
Accrington, Harwood, Padiham, Chorley, nesting
-
den, Clitheroe, Ramshottom, Clayton-le-Moors,
Burnley, Nelson, and Stockport.

Mr. W. Carr, Cherley, who presided, said the ,
principal question which the operatives had to
deal with at the present time was the nine hours'
movement, and in spite of the opinion of the
Chamber of Commerce magnates he did not be-
lieve that cotton operatives were in as good a
position as they ought to be. In Germany and
Belgium, as well as in England, working men were
battling for their rights. In England they worked
peaceably, with moral means and public opinion
on their side; but on the continent they would,
by-and-bye, hear the "thug of the bullet and the
slash of the bayonet.," It was not his wish that
it should be so, but he would that capitalists
would see to it. They must let Parliament know
that they wanted it for their wives, who had to
work at the mill, leaving behind them a disconso-
late home and seeing their children nursed by tho
stranger.

Mr. James White, of Church, reviewed the
position of the united Society and the work it had
done in the district. From the close of the Comae
strike, which ended disastrously to the operatives,
on account of the American civil war, up to the
present time they had done much to raise the

Without stales they had in many districts brought

was only one district at the present time (that was
Burnley) where they wanted educating, and they
had a schoolmaster in their secretary who wild
educate the masters of Burnley up to the standard
list. The great question they had to press forward
was the nine hours movement.

employed at two of the principal works came to

LEAMINGTON.
SUCCESSFUL STRIKE OF LIBOURERS.
On Tuesday the builders' labourers struck at
Leamington for an advance of wages from 4d. to
41d. per hour, equivalent to a rise of 2s. 4d. per
week. The labourers had given notice which
expired last Saturday, and, as the masters had not
conceded their den:lamb on Tuesday they refused to
work. The principal builders held a meeting on
Tuesday afternoon and resolved to grant the re-

agreed to resume work. The strike stopped the
bricklayers and plasterers, and suspended business.
Labourers received 18s, 10d., and will now have a
guinea and twopence.

TILE STRIKE OF OPERATIVE /WINNERS.

. -
A fortnight has now passed away, and still there
is no seteement of this difficulty. Those prejudiced
persons that prophecied the surrender of the men
before this time have been miserably dew ived.
Two or three of the factories have commenced

Your humble correspondent is of opinion, Sir,

The Nottingham spinners, and other soeietios,

them. Last week they sent 'something over
£3O, and this, week I ,believe from £6O to
£7O will be sent for the men; and their
energies in helping to collect for the
women and children deserves special mention,
as it is characteristic of the usual goodheartedness
and love of justice that we can ever trace in the
manners and doings of the working classes of
Nottingham. Should the masters triumph in this
' struggle —which is decidedlyimprobable--..what will
they win? What credit can they over give t 3
themselves in being .the cause of distress., and
suffering for the sake of scarcely two farthings an
hour? Oh! what an honour it will be. To what
a climax of dignity our groat manufacturers are

trades unions and the hand and heart manner in

wlaioh do working classes lean together, they will

fair day's wages for a fair day's work in the

TUE FIFTY-POUR MOUES MOVEMENT IN TIIE

COTTON TRADE.

A meeting of delegates representing the cotton
operatives of the four counties of Yorkshire, Lan-
cashire, Cheshire, and Derbyshire, was held in
Manchester on Sunday, to take into consideration
the present aspect of the 54 hours movement.
There were 82 delegates in attendance, repre-
senting sixty districts and organised associations.
After transacting the ordinary routine business
it was announced that the President of the Exe-
cutive Council for securing the 54 hours move-
ment (blr. Thomas Law) had found it necessary,
from pressure of other business, to resign his
office. The resignation was accepted, and Mr.
William Leigh, of Hyde, elected in his place.
The Secretary (Mr. Mawdsloy) read a statement
of the efforts taken in regard to the question of
reducing the hours of labour since the last meet-
ing, and the general opinion expressed at the
meeting was that Mr. Mundella's bill was making
satisfactory progress.
At a former meeting it was resolved that the
Executive Committee, or delegates appointed by
the Committee, should wait upon the whole of the
members of Parliament—whether borough or
county—in the four counties over which the
organisation extends, to ascertain their views on
the 54 hours qdltation, and to solicit their
sympathy and support to the Bill Mr. Mundella
and others have taken in hand. The delegates
reported that the members had been waited upon;
that the majority had testified their approval of
the measure, which they promised to support;
others unconnected with the trade asked for infor-
mation, while some few refused to entertain the
matter in any way, ulleging as the ground of
objection that the smart foreign competition with
which we have to contend renders it inadvisable
to meddle with the hours of labour in factories.

A Parliamentary Committee was appointed, who
will be sent to London to use all means in their
power, by personal interviews, &e., with members
of both Houses of Parliament, to promote the
passing of Mr. Mundella's Bill.

A well-attended meetillg of millowners was
held on Tuesday, in the Chamber of Commerce,
Belfast, to consider the subject of the threatened
strike. The demand of the workers is 4s. per
week extra. The millowners have offered 2s.
extra, which the men, meantime, refuse. The
millowners at the meeting unanimously resolved to
refuse compliance with the men's demands, and to
have a general lock-out after Saturday, if the men
already on strike do not return to work and those
who have given notice withdraw it, and accept the
masters' terms. The agitation, which commenced
with the 111 x-dressers, has extended to almost

was then told that he might "go to the Society
and see what it would do for him," or words to
that effeat ; a week's wages being paid .to hint in
lieu of notice, and an order given that he was "not
to show his face in the yard again." The recital
of the facts elicited expressions of great indignation
and contempt for the offending official who had
acted in this despotic manner, the unanimous senti-
ment being that if such arbitrary proceedings were
persisted in the-whole of the Men along the North
London line would leave- work until the superin-
tendent were himself removed. After an address
from the Chairman, which was frequently inter-
rupted by applause, a resolution to the following
effect was carried with acclamation That this
meeting of railway • servants employed in the
Camden Station respectfully, but indignantly, -pro-
test against the 'Arbitrary conduct of Mr. Jones,
the superintendent, as an unwarrantable interfer.
ence with the personal liberties of the men, and
that right of free speech, which is the pride of
every British subject ; and this meeting is of
opinion that such treatment, if submitted to with-
out protest., is calculated to degrade the self-
respect of the men themselves, and to inj ore the
company by causing general irritation against those
in authority over them." The motion having been
declared to be carried, another was proposed,

seconded, and carried uraminously :---" That the
chairman be requested to eonvey this resolution to
the Chairman of the Company, and request the
consideration uf the case of Mr. Tarbox by the
Directors." Several speeches were delivered,
showing the inclination of the managers to inter-
fere with the liberties of the men in their leisure
hours, and a proposal was then made "that a levy
should be raised under the direction of the com-
mittee, who should pay Mr. Tarbox his wages
until ha were reinstated or provided with
another situation." At least fifty men jumped
to their feet to second this resolution, which was

subsequently extended so as to apply to the eases
of any other men who might be dismissed in like
manner. This proposal was carried with loud

cheers, and several hundred names of parties ready
to make weekly contributions were banded in.
About fifty pounds was said to have been
guaranteed in this way at once.
A railway servant from Poplar having addressed
the nieeting, a resolution was carried, "That all
those present should at once join the Amalgamated
Society of Railway Servants." (Loud applause.)
One of the men from Broad-street Station
reported that he had been in like manner threatened
to be discharged for having attended these meet-
bogs, but he had warned the manager that if the
threat was put in force, the whole of the men
in his department were prepared to leave
their work. (Prolonged cheering, and cries of
We will! we will!) He believed that the
whole of the men along the line would turn out
rather than submit to such tyranny. (Applause.)
Following these resolutions was a vote of thanks
to the chairman, which was carried with extra-

ordinary enthusiasm, 1 and a vote of gratitude to
Mr. M. T. Bass, M.P., for his sympathy for rail-
way men, which last led to a scene of excitement
rarely witnessed in a public meeting; the ,whole
assembly, densely crowded as it was, rose, and
the chairman having been called to honour the
vote by giving the "Kentish fire," led the meet-
ing in such style as shook the building.
PLIMMEAD BRANCIL—The regular meeting ot
this Branch tdok place on Monday week awl was
well attended. Several applications for member-
ship were made, and a desire to open a branch at
Stroud by an energetic railwayman. Mr. Chap-
man, General Secretary, was present and addressed
the meeting. The Railway Service Gazette was
condemned in severe terms. The reports in the
BER-111VE gave great satisfitetion. Votes of thanks
to Mr. Bass, M.P., Dr. Baxter Langley and Mr.
Chapman closed the business of the evening.
BEIIMONDEMY.—The adjourned meeting was held
at the Railway Tavern; St. James's-street, on
Friday week. There waS was a good attendance,
and the numbers enrolled during the evening was
most encouraging. The General Secretary gave a
statement of the number of members and finances,
and also explained the nature of the conference of
Saturday the 27th ult., and the result arrived at.
Votes of thanks to Mr. T. Bass, Esq., M.P., Dr.
Langley, the Chairman, and General Secretary,
terminated the business of the.meeting.

AICALGA.MA.TED SOCIETY OP RA.ILWAY SERYA.NTS
—The weekly meeting of the Executive Council
was held at the Winchester Arms, Southwark-
street, on Tuesday evening last; Dr. J. Baxter
Langley presiding. About thirty delegates, repre-
senting duly constituted branches, were present.
The general secretary made a report of the meetings
attended by the chairman and himself since the
last council, and read numerous applications for
visits in the- future to which replies were
authorised. A mass of correspondence was then
• read, raising many important points of detail, com-
plaining of tho conduct of the Editor of the Railway
Service Gazette in the publication of his libellous
attacks, which were universally condemnednot only
as directly false in fact, but as most injurious to the
progress of the union of the men. Several branches
complained of the suppression of their reports, and
pointed with satisfaction to the superior reports
of the Bar..-HrvE, and the impartial attitude of
that paper. Branehes were reported as having
been formed at Camden, Paddington, Kentish
Town, Poplar, Bow, Stourbridge, Cardiff, New-
castle-en-Tyne, Barnsley, Rystead, Kilburn,
Pontypool, Peterborough, 'Nino Elms, Strood,
Kingsland, Aldgate, whilst ahem Were: in ennrsn
of establishment. The Chairman read letters
from Mr. Graham, which were most cordially re-
ceived, and a vote of confidence in that gentleman
adopted unanimously. Ho also reported as to
several meetings be had attended. Lists for
the purposes of collecting the levy were ordered,
and a resolution passed to the effect "that the eoun •
cil much regretted to find that many societies of
railway men had been established by gentlemen
who had been employed to promote the union of
the men, but that no reports of the formation of

these societies had been received from the persons

establishing thorn; that the council were desirous
of being placed in friendly alliance with all these
societies, and regretted that any appearance of in-
difference should have been produced by the ne-

glect of the parties referred to in communicating
with head-quarters. The council invite all such
societies to communicate with them, either through
Mr. Graham or Mr. Chapman, and formally to
join the Amalgamated Society so as to be in a
position to send a delegate to the ensuing
conference." Several resolutions were pro-
proposed to the effect that Mr. Bass should be
requested to remove the present editor of the
Railway Service Gazette, but the, chairman advised
a policy of peace, explaining that he bad sent a
letter to the Gazette which he trusted would put
an end to further, misimpressions, and which the
' editor had promised to insert on the following
Saturday. [This letter will be found in our
columns to-day.] He advised the parties to wait
to see whether justice would be done, and they
then had the remedy in their own hands if they
could not obtain fair play. The General Secretary
having been instructed to send copies of the
programme for the delegate meeting to certain
applicants, the meeting adjourned for a fort-
night.

RAILWAY Orpassato:kr.--Cases are reported of
arbitrary interference with the freedom of railway
men at Brighton, Cardiff, Wellingborough and
other places. The other employes have resolved
to stand by their mates. We shall be glad to
publish the details of such cases wherever they
occur.

restored to health to be coniseious of having

received a memorial from the men four months
ago, and that he has promised to attend to the

MERTHYR TYDVIL. The members of this
branch met in strong force on the 30th uhinto.
The Rev. Canon Jenkins, D.D., took the chair,
and made an excellent and telling speech, inviting
all to join the Society and support the present
movement—viz., lesa hours of labour, more pay,

mised his best support to the cause, and expressed
the pleasure it gave him in presiding over them

hope that railway servants would see the value of
the institution and - become members of the

was loudly cheered.
Votes of thanks to M. T. Bass, Esq., M.P., the

secretary, closed the meeting.

The following is the Bill prepared by the com-
mittee and entrusted to Mr. W. Vernon Harcourt,
Mr. 'Henry James, Mr. A. J. Mundella, and Mr.
George Melly, whose names are on the back of
the Bill. -

CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1871

AMENDMENT. • .
A BILL TO AMEND THE PROVISIONS OF THE " CRI-
MINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1871,". RELATING
TO MOLESTATION. .

Whereas it is expedient to amend the provisions
of the Act of the 34th and 35th of her Majesty,
chapter 32, entitled "An Act to Amend the
Criminal Law telating to Violence, Throats, and
Molestation."

•' Bo it enacted by the Queen's most evcellent
majesty, by and with the consent of the Lords
Spiritual and Temporal and Commons in this
present Parliament assembled, and by the authority
of the same, as follows :-
1. The first section of the Act of the 34th and
35th of Her Majesty, chapter thirty-two, entitled
"An Act to Amend the Criminal Law Relating to
Violence, Threats, and Molestation," shall be
repealed, and instead thereof it shall be enacted as
follows, viz.:

Every person who does any of the following
acts, with the view as hereinafter mentioned, that
is to say, who

(1.) Uses violence to any person, or to the pro-
perty of any other person; or
(2.) Threatens or intimidates any other person
in such manner as would justify a justice of
the peace (on complaint made to such justice)
in binding over to keep the peace tho person
so threatening or intimidating; or
(3.) Molests or obstructs any other person
(a.) By persistently following him from place
to place, or
(b.) By following him in or through any street
or road with two or more persons in a dis-
orderly manner, or
(o.) By ihiding him or depriving him of, or
hindering him in the use of, any tools,
clothes, or property, owned or used by

him, or
(d.) By acts, calculated to intimidate him,

with a view in the case of any such acts as afore-
said thereby to coerce such other person.
(1.) Being a master, to atomise or to cease to
employ any workman, or being a workman to
quit any employment, or to return work be-
fore it is finished;
(2.) Being a master not to offer, or being a
workman not to accept, any employment or
work;

(3.) Being a master or workman, to belong or
not to belong to any tomporory or permanent
association or combination;
(4.) Being a master or workman, to pay any fine
or penalty imposed by any temporary or per-
manent association or combination;
(5.) Being a master, to alter the mode of carry-
on his business, or the number or description
of any persons employed by him,
shall be liable to imprisonment, with or without
hard labour, for a term not exceeding three
months. .

Nothing in this section shall prevent any person
from being liable under any other Act, or otherwise,
to any other or higher punishment than is pro-
vided for any offence by this section; so that no
person be punished twice for the same offence.
Provided that no person shall be liable to any
punishment for doing or conspiring to do any act
on the ground that such act restrains or tends to
restrain the free course of trade, unless such act is
one of the acts herein-before specified in this
section, and is done with the object of coercing
herein-before mentioned.

The said Act shall be construed as if the pro-
visions of this Act were substituted for first section
of the said Act.

Several loading statesman, on both sides of the
House, have expressed their concurrence with the
Bill as proposed, and are prepared to support it.

THE LONDON CARPENTERS .b.ND
THE NINE HOURS MOVEMENT.

On Tuesday night an aggregate meeting of 00
operative carpenters and joiners, includiag both
.society and non-society men, was held in St.
James's Hall, for the purpose of deciding on the
means to be adopted to enforce the terms Pf the
memorial lately submitted to the master buildete
of the metropolis, and which embodied the follow-
ing demands: via., the establishment of a code of
working rules, to be drawn up by a united com—
mittee of masters and workmen, for the regula-
tion of the trade in the London district; the re-
chidden of the hours of labour to nine per day, or
fifry-oneper week, including six hours on Sato;'-f-
days ; and an advance in the rate of Wages from
Bd. to 9d, per hour. These demands had hese
refused by the master builders, and they had also
-declined to receive a• deputation from the eat*
penters to discuss the claims. The hall Was
crowded
Mr. Lloyd Jones occupied the chair, and opened
the proceedings by an address on the econonlieal
phase of the question, contending that the men
were perfectly justified in their endeavours to
attain the objects they desired.
Mr. Watkin, the secretary, then read a memerial
which had been sent to the master builder's.
The demands of the meu, as stated in the me-
niorial, are,---lst., That a code of working rules,
for the guidance of both employers and employe&
he established in the London' district, and that
the employers be asked to co-operate with the
men in drawing up such a code of rules. 2ndly.
That the working hours be nine per day, from
Monday to Friday, with six hours on Saturday,
making 51 hours per week; and, thirdly, that
the rate of wages be 91 instead of' Bcl. per hour.
Mr. Wright moved the first resolution : •
"That this meeting fully approves of the course
taken by the delegates from the carpenters and
joiners in the London district, in the memorial to
the employers for a reduction of the hours of
labour from ten to nine hours a day, and for an
advance in the wages from Bd. to 9d. an hour."
Mr. Panchen seeonded the resolution, which was
supported by
Mr. Harry, Secretary of the Amalgamated
Society of Carpenters and Joiners, and adopted
unanimously.

Mr. Sadler, chairman of the delegates meeting,
read the proposed code of rules, the principles of
which were, that. the hours of work should. be
nine per day except Saturday, when they
should be six hours, making 51 hours per week;

that the wages be 9d. pex hour; that overtime

paid for at the rate of time and a half, and double
after certain hours, but be discountenanced; that
piecework be totally abolished in the London
district; that no alteration be made in these rules
without six months' notice; and that any proposed
alteration be submitted to the arbitration of an
equal number, of masters and men. He concluded
by moving the following resolution :
"That this meeting ill of opinion that the code
of working rules just read is in every respect suit-
able for the better regulation of our trade in the
London district, and h9pe it will be accepted by
the employers, believing it to be necessary for
,trutintaining a friendly feeling between employers
and employed."
Mr. Hillier seconded the resolution, which was
supported by Mr. Buckland, and carried unani-
mously.

The Secretary then read a.correspondence which
had taken place between him and Mr. Piper, the
secretary of the Builders' Society, from which it
appeared that the memorial was submitted to a
meeting of the Builders' Society held at the Free-
masons' Tavern, on the 29th February, and Mr.
Piper was directed to forward to the memorialists
a copy of the reply they had given to a similar
memorial from the operative stonemasons. This
reply was to the effect that any diminution in the
hours of labour during the summer months would
cause great inconvenience; that the present work-
ing hours did not exceed on the average 64 hours
per week; that wages in the building trade had
been increased three times in the last ton years;
and that no cause had been shown for an increase,
and neither did the state of the building trade
justify such a step. At a meeting of delegates
held on the 9th March they passed a resolution
requesting the master builders to meet a deputation
from them to discuss the 'matter; but the masters,
at a subsequent meeting, passed a resolution
declining this offer, and stating that it did not
appear to them that any further consideration viss
likely to be of 'advantage. • '`

Three letters which had been received from
building firms were then read. One of them from
Air. Sage, Gray's Inn-road, expressing his
sympathy with the movement and announcing his
intention to comply with the requirements of the
men, comtnencing under the new arangements un
the Ist of July. Another letter was from Air.
Sapwell, stating that as far as he was perflOnallY

conce.rned he would be happy to accede to the
terms, but that he could make no actual promise
till he•knew what would be done by the trade
generally. The third letter was from Mr. John
Woodward, who said he thought fifty-hours a week
and £1 18s. 3d. wages 'would have been complied
with freely.
Mr. Sinclair then moved the following resolu-
tion:—

---- •
"That this meeting views with dissatisfaction
and regret the position taken by, the Master
Builders' Society in refusing to receive a deputa-
tion from the carpenters and joiners of London to
discuss the terms of their memorial, witb
the view of coming to an amicable settlement,
having thus ignored our claims and disregarded
our overtures, leaving us the only alternative for
adopting the necessary means for enforcing what
we believe to be a just and reasonable demand;
and this meeting is of opinion that we should take
action on the Ist of Juno, by ceasing work in such
firms as the delegates shall decide, unless in the
meantime the employers makdknown their willing-
ness to accede to our demands; and we hereby
pledge ourselvea to give all the moral and pecuniary
aid in our power for the furtherance of the move-
ment."
The resolution having been seconded by Mr.
Smith, and supported by Ms. T. Marten, it was put
to the meeting and carried amid loud cheering.
The proceedings terminated with a vote of
thanks to the Chairman.

AN APPEAL FOR DORSET LABOURERS
ON STRIKE.

A strike having taken place at Milborno St.
Andrew, because the masters refused to advance
3s. on Os. per week, funds for the support of these
men and their families are herewith respectfully
solicited. P. 0.0. or stamps may be sent to Thos.
Martin, Secretary to the Relief Fund, Milborne,
Blandford.

APPEAL.-1 beg to draw your urgent attention
to the following facts in connection with the strike
of the labourers in the parish of Milborne St.
Andrew :—A few weeks ago about 40 of the men
(copying the example of their brethren in War-
wickshire) determined to make an effort for an '
increase on their miserable pittance of Os. per
week. They accordingly called a meeting, and
drew up a respecfal memorial to their employers,
asking for a rise of 3s. and a reduction of an
hour per week. The farmers, exasperated at the

as a natural consequence, about one-half of them

half of the remainder, who are still on strike, and
whose condition is lamentable in the extreme, that
I take the liberty of addressing you. The poor
fellows are actually in want of bread, and unless
something is done, they will be compelled to drop
the agitation. They are without a leader, and in
a terrible fix. Being a native of the county, I'
know from Personal observation that the present
state of the labourer is truly deplorable. I have
endeavoured to do what I can for the poor men,
but being single-handed, my efforts are povrerless.

papers, but caunot obtain any assistance. Will
your League act as ptehntly as possible in the

the men will doubtless be able to bring the strike

THE MANCHESTER POSTMEN.

seni. a full report of the meeting o

Manchester postmen. The men have been shame-
fully treated, in fact, their claims have been
totally ignored, and everything relating to their
wants and welfare overlooked.

The Birmingham mon have met with similar
treatment. This is only a sample of how the
Post-Office treat their servants generally.
The transfer of the telegraphs to the State took
place sth of February, 1870. Since then and up
to the present time the clerks have had repeated
promises made thorn that the classifications would
be issued shortly. After waiting over two years
we are still without the long-expected settlement.
The conduct of the chief officials during and
after the telegraphists strike was more in accord-
ance with the rules of a country governed by
despotic laws. The system carried out tends to
produce hypocrisy, deceit, and cringing servility.
We are strangers to the independence and freedom
enjoyed by trades unionists. The promotions are
generally made by selection, which is often a
great injustice to those who are not prepared to
swallow any pill prepared for, them. The Post
Office is a hot-bed of favouritism and inconsis-
tencies. This is carried on to such an extent as
to produce general discontent and disgust every- '
where. We shall never mend this unsatisfactory
state of things till the whale of the staff combine
together for the purpose of forming a union. At
the present time we are denied the right of com-
bination, although trades unions are legal. Surely
the servants of the Civil Service cannot long be
denied the rights of their fellow-citizens. I trust
we shall be able to make it a question at the nest
general election, and that the trades unions will
lend us their support by putting the question to
candidates soliciting their votes—" Are you wil-
ling to aid and assist the withdrawal of the rule
denying civil servants the right of forming a
union?" Unless this, is done, we shall always be
at the mercy of those place 1 over us, however just,
our cause may
.be. At the preseut time, anyone
joining the Pest-Office servioe must be prepared to
sell his mind, body and soul, to a tyraunical sys-
tem, which is thoroughly detested throughout
Great Britain and Ireland.

It would be doing some good if a member of
Parliament would move for returns showing the
scale of wages paid at all towns; afro the amount
allowed in sickness, the mode of pay during sick-
ness, which ought to be performed with regu-
larity.
The Factory Act has been greatly extended of
late, the hours of duty performed at branch offices
is frequently, twelve per day„ with no. ovettirne.

BA.TURDAY, MAY 18, 1872.

THE THREATENED STRIKE OF THE
LONDON CARPENTERS.
The meeting of the Carpenters and Joiners
in St. James's Hall on Tuesday night last, at
which Mr. LtoYD JONES presided, for num-
bers, zeal, and unanimity, loft nothing to be

desired.
The demands made by the men as to time
and wages are important demands, and they
seem to be made in a strong consciousness of
their reasonableness. Those who are in the
habit of discussing such demands from the
employers' point of view, usually have a good
deal to say when the men ask what they con-
sider "too much," but they never condescend
to define the limits of "too little" or "too
much." They never attempt to point out
what is really " enough " and no more; what
might be given, and what ought to be given,
as a really satisfying quantity. Under these
circumstances the men must take the matter
into their own hands. They must say under
what conditions they will sell their labour
and at what price, per hour, per day, or by
the year. Whether the price they fix
is, or is not, enough to keep their
families well-housed, clad, and fed, is a
matter, the mass of the people will not trouble
their heads about. If they support their
wives and children respectably, the general
public will cry "so much the better." If
they fail to do this and swell the pauper ranks
in the country, the cry will be " so much the
worse.'' Men in the grass take things as they
are, and bear the suffering from whioh
they themselves are exempt, with admirable
fortitude.
When a poor sethpstress has been starved
to death, and a coroner's jury tells us plainly
that this occurred because of insufficient re-
muneration for work, very little fuss is made
about the matter, though everybody is per-
fectly well aware that there are thousands
upon thousands whose wages are the same,
whose misery is unendurable, whose destiny,
though more quietlyconsummated, is precisely
the same. Where such things go on daily,
who can doubt the duty of working men to
look after themselves, to get as much for their
labour as they reasonably can, and thus
secure themselves from the many evils of
poverty. _ _

- But in doing this it must be borne in mind
that there are times and seasons
when every kind of commodity is of less value
in the market than at others. There are
times to rise and times to fall, and working
men must look out and prepare for these fluc-
tuations and act wisely in reference to them.
Carpenters and joiners have not much to

fear from "foreign competition," and though
a great deal has been said about Swedish im-
portations of finished work the scare has gone
by without much damage to anybody. There
is not a great deal to fear just now on that
head—nevertheless suocess in this projected
strike will demand every necessary precaution.
The men throughout the country will re quire
to give it their hearty approval, and their un-
divided and vigorous support. There must be
no discord amongst leaders, no clashing ill
council; no half-hearted. hanging back any-
where. This demand of itself is but part of a
great labour movement, destined to advance
or throw back the cause of the worker in
exact proportion to the carefulness and , skill
with which it is handled. Ninepence per hour,
and fifty-one hours per working week form a
considerable advance favourable to the men,
and they are not likely to get these without a
severe struggle; and if they see good reasons
why they should enter on this, it should be
with a disposition not to give ground for a
moment'till their victory is won.
It would be a grave disaster if this battle
should be lost. Every attempt to advance
should (tarry with it the power to do so; and
every trade that fails to do this should be held
answerable by the whole army of labour.
Once the fight has been entered on, vigorous
action, and not loose talk will be needed;
whilst in their demeanor towards their em-
ployers the men should always show a dispo-
sition to settle their difference in a conciliatory
and friendly spirit. However, if the decisions
of Tuesday's meeting be carried out by the
men, an amicable settlement will have to be
speedily made, or a bitter contest entered on.
We advise the first, if at all practicable; if
not, then a fair stand-up dogged English
fight. Everything on both sides done openly
in the daylight. Should this be the spirit
displayed, as we trust it will, then we think
the carpenters and joiners of the London dis-
trict should come out victorious.

articles.title: WAR DEMON.
articles.text:
THE WAR DEMON.

THE speech of Due D'AUDRIFFET PASQUIER,
in the French National Assembly, though too
old for newspaper comment, suggests a thought
which may be worth expressing in reference
to the future peace of Europe. That the late
French Emperor's Government ;was rotten to
its centre scarcely needed the evidence ad-
duced ; nobody but the corrupt, the ignorant
and selfish in France ever believed in it,
whilst in England the stupid crowd who
respect only success, and who always bow to
thrones, were its chief admirers. nuc
PAI3QUIER has given chapter and verse for his
charges, so that even the stupidest can scarcely
regard it any longer, but as a stupendous and
most disgusting fraud.
We must not forget, however, that the chief
regret felt by the French people is, not that
they sought to help the ambition of such a
charlatan as the third BONAPA.BTE ; not that the
curse of war was lightly and rashly sanctioned
by them; but rather that the frauds of the
EMPEROR and his ministers had prevented
them from being in a state of prepared-
ness; and that when they went out
to seek for glory they found only defeat,
disaster, and disgrace. If they had won
instead of losing; if their scamp of an
Eurxnon had returned to Paris at the head of
victorious legions, instead of running away
and biding himself like the poor paltroon he
is, they would have strewed his path with
flowers, and sung his praises as the mightiest
monarch of the world.

And what, it may be asked, was the recom-
mendation of Duo PASQUIER that excited
most the enthusiasm of his audience? Simply
the recommendation of what may be regarded
as the universal arming of France, The
drilling of the young men of the country;
the preparing of the rising generations of
France for effectual slaughter-work when the
hour arrives for another grim dance of death.
Looked at soberly, this simply means per-
manent wars in Europe; at least it means
France fully armed,' Germany fully armed,
England with a huge standing army, and a
drain on her resources for warlike expenditure
which must abridge the bread in every poor
man's house.

The whole of Europe is inevitably in for a
military futuro with all WI ftecompanying

evils and horrors. Emperors and. Kings have
their little game to play, and they will play it,
whatever it may cost. The prosperity, the
progress, the peace of the world, is nothing to
them. Domestic thrift, comfort, happiness,
are quite subordinate considerations, and as
for Christian humility and fraternal affection,
they are simple old-fashioned dhams which
have given place to the nightmares of modern
policy, including a feverish ambition for R oya
conquest.

We do not say that nations should be afraid
to fight in a good cause, or that men
should draw back or stand still when
the cause of right or justice were in
need of defence. But the masses of the people
should, we think, absolutely refuse to shed
each other's blood at the bidding of rulers
who care nothing for the lives of their people,
whoa they have ambitious personal objects to
serve. If this madness be not put a stop to by
public opinion in free countries, it never will
come to an end, and it is quite time now in
this nineteenth century of Christian preaching,
that Christian truth and civilization should
overcome the Pagan brutality of kings and
emperors urged into sanguinary action by
their intriguing counsellors.

HAPPY PROSPECTS' FOR ENGLAND
AND AMERICA.
Timm is something in the very sound of
common sense which apprises us of its having
been spoken. Nearly two months ago, Mr.
JOHN STUART MILL said, "If there is any
value at all in the principle of international
arbitration, there is surely no subject to
which that principle can be more fittingly
applied than to determining the true sense of
an international engagement. We may re-
gret that this method of settling national
differences should be subjected to so severe a
trial at so early a period of its history; but
we should not be therefore justified in repu-
diating it in one of the very cases which
require it most." Singularly enough, how-
ever, this honest and sensible deliverance did
not reach the general ear till Lord GuAxviur,
and. Mr. GLADSTONE had communicated to
Parliament the progress and present state of
thenegociationsbetwoon England and America.
Simultaneously a telegram from Washington
announces a probable compromise by which
an additional article or a supplementary treaty
will release both Powers from liability for
indirect damages incase of future infringements
on neutrality. This, in fact, is the point to
which the ministerial statements to the two
Houses really came.
Meanwhile, the most reliable information
through private sources on the other side,
most fully confirms the grounds of hesitancy
attributed on this side by skille4 observers to
the GRANT Cabinet. Mr. Fair, we are told,
has always been ready to surrender the cense-
uential olaims ; but it did not suit the views
of President GRANT, with an eye to his re-
election. A short experience, however, has con-
vinced him that ho had mistaken the feeling
of his fellow citizens when he took it
for granted that to bully England
was the best way of gaining his
end. The American people, as we always
thought, never seriously expected any such
payment as that claimed. On the contrary,
the satisfaction with the conclusion of a treaty
introduoing the principle of arbitration was
so general and strong, that even some sacrifice
of first expectations would not have been
deemed too dear a price for the advantage.
But General GRANT is something like our IRON
DUKE, like in hardness, but, luckily, like in
malleability btoo. Thus it is that some men
ascertain the strength of public opinion—by
resisting it till they find it becoming irre-
sistible, and then yielding to it. Sometimes
they avoid the appearance of surrendering
upon compulsion, but sometimes they do net.
"If this new plan result in a settlement,"
writes a well-informed correspondent in New
York, "it will be cordially accepted in this
country, though it will injure Mr. FISII and
the PRESIDENT, not SO much, because they
have yielded, as because they took a position
they were not able to maintain."
What Lord GRANVILLE and Mr. GLADSTONE
told Parliament before it rose and adjourned
for Whitsuntide, was, that their proposal of

a supplementary article, as above described,
had, according to rule, been submitted for ap-
proval to the Senate, with which therefore it
now rests. Possibly, even before this sheet
goes to press, the result of that constitutional
reference may be credibly, though notofficially,
known. The result, let us hope, will be such
as to satisfy Earl RUSSELL himself, in his
patriotic jealousy, praiseworthy though it may
have been thought less judicious. The principle
of international arbitration is a great principle
and, once adopted, will, we trust, be fruit-
ful in amity and peace all the world over.
"England and America," to • conclude with
the concluding words of the P.RDEE MINISTER,
of the former country, "undertook a groat
responsibility in the face of all other nations,
when they attempted to apply, after some
recent discourapments, this principle of •
amicable settlement to a great controversy
between two high-spirited nations. If these
two nations succeed in giving effect to what
undoubtedly is the desire sincerely entertained,
and cordially entertained, alike •on the one
side and on the other, something, I think,
will have been achieved for the benefit of the
cause of peace. If, on the other hand, they
should fail, however the case may stand as
between the parties, they conjointly will suffer
great discredit in the face of all other civilised
nations, and their failure in this great effort of
peaceful settlement will be nothing less, in
our judgment, than a misfortune to mankind.
The result can hardly be otherwise than
decisive, and I hope it is not a sign of too
sanguine a temper on my part if I venture to
say there is every probability that we may be
enabled to recognise it as honourable and
happy,"

PRINCE BISMARCK AND THE PAPACY.
Tin: last thing done by the Gorman chan-
cellor before retiring to the country for the
benefit of his health, was another of his
master strokes in policy. Germany being the
only one of the European Powers not repre-
sented by envoy at the Court of the Vatican,
Prince BISMSRCK selected to supply the lack
Cardinal, Prince HounsLonn, When first
apprised of this appointment, the Cardinal
Secretary of State took no notice of the
communication. After waiting a week in vain,
the German resident in Rome was ordered to
jog ANTONELLI'S memory, who answered that,
as Prince 11011ENLOHE was announced as
coming, ho had. not thought it needful to
acknowledge the intimation. This was
like the man, who, having first put forward
this fetch, added that his HouNliss, while per-
fectly sensible of the EMPEROR'S intentions,
was nevertheless, in present circumstances,
under the necessity of declining to authorise
Prince HOIIIINLOECE, who being a Cardinal, is
subject to the Pope, to accept the important
and delicate mission which had been confided.
to him as a Prince of the German Empire.
If the POPE and his secretary are content
with this assertion of the supremacy of the
Church over State, Prince BISUIRCK, we may
be sure, will make him welcome to it. Ho
has got rid of the awkwardness of Germany
being the only great Power without a represen-
tative at the Vatican, and the Vatican is itself
loaded with the odium of having rejected. an
envoy who, from his eminent ecclesiastical rank,
ought to have been most acceptable:of all. The
simple fact, however, is that Prince HOIIENLOHE
comes nearer to sympathising with the "Old.
Catholics' than with the " Ultramontanos,"
and was, presumably, selected for the post on
this very account. He left Rome for Germany
of his own accord, from disgust with what ho
saw of the Papal counoils. Nevertheless, he
was quite ready to servo as ambassador if the
POPE would receive him. As it is, the Ger-
man Catholics may now, if they like, send up
a serious grievance to the Head of their
Church. What effect the approach of Cardinal
HOIIENLOHE, as representative of victorious
and. united Germany, to the Pontiff's private
ear, might have had upon affairs of Church
and State, it is now vain to speculate or oon-
j ohm.
With one foot, as it were, upon the train,
Prince Basuuck,before leav lug Berlin,deolared
publicly that the dogma lately promulgated by
the Holy Sae rendered. it impossible to act in
armony with the Curia, To restore peace

among the denominations, it appeared neces-

conscience. The rejection of an Envoy was
not a frequent occurrence, and had not
happened to him before during a diplomatic
career of twenty-one years. It pained him
the more, as Cardinal 1101rENLOIIE was fitted
to bring about a conciliatory feeling. Sorrow,
however, did not justify irritation. Regard
for the interests of the Catholic population of
Germany determined him to nominate another

the CARDINAL, and Aoubtful ss he was of
another achieving equally good results. At
any rate, ho should always reject any treaty
with Rome in which the Papacy might claim
that certain State laws should not be binding
upon a portion of the subjects of the Empire.
A. motion for striking out the estimate for an

articles.text:
MR. GLADSTONE ON RELIGION AND
SCIENCE.

AT a meeting of the friends to King's Col-
lege, London, Mr. ainstoNE made a speech
of a very temperate and lucid description,
referring to the supposed, but mistakenly
supposed, opposition between religion and
science. Admitting, he said, the incapacity
of his underitanding to grasp the full purport
of what has taken place with respect to the
Infallibility decree at Rome, it yet appeared
to him a proclamation of war against
the progress of the human mind. On the
other hand, what did he see among ourselves?
Not speaking of the uninstructed classes, he
saw on drawing-rooni tables works that speak
of Christianity as an antiquated superstition.
In one work of great interest and ability, the
writer, discussing the manner in which, in
groat crises of human history, individuals
have arisen of great gifts and powers, says
that their apparition is so remarkable that
it .would have been perfectly allowable to
term it providential in pre-historic times.
In his view, then, there was a time when
mankind were so ignorant that they might,
without forfeiting the title of rational crea-
tures, believe in Providence. But another
and greater power has arisen, which, under
tho name of Science, has gone to war with
Providence, so that we live in an age when
Providence is no longer to be treated as other
than an idle dream. Now this, says Mr.
OLIDSTONE, is not science at all. It is a rash,
precipitate, narrow, self-informed manner of
dealing with subjects; and would shut us up

to one of two terrible alternatives—either to
give up the investigation of nature, or to give
up all hope in the world that is unseen. A.
more terrible imposture, concluded the PRE-
MIER, never threatened the happiness of man-
kind.

articles.title: SPAIN.
articles.text:
SPAIN.

TIIE Carlists in Spain are not entirely put
down; but, as they have hitherto met with
nothing but defeat, their complete defeat may
be anticipated. In Navarre they have entirely
succumbed; and they will not, most probably, ,
have better success in Biscay. Beaton there,
nothing will remain for them but dispersion
over the country or flight across the frontier
into France. DON CARLOS was overweening
enough to expect that RODA, first made chief
in command, would seize the strongholds of
Pampelina and San Sebastian, and, since he
failed to possess himself of those points of
support, the PRETENDER put li.ouftinE in his
place; at the present, however, with no symptoms
of better success. The double cry of the aspiring
PRINCE is, Down with the foreigner and Up
with the altar ; and there are some
two hundred priests actually in the field.
But, as we know, the first result of the now
commander was his total route by General Mo.
RIONES, who made the PRETENDER fly for his
life, and took, it now appears, not many fewer
than a thousand prisoners. The best reliance
of the insurgents is on the fanatical tendencies
of the women and the vain() set by the peasantry
of the Basque provinces upon their ancient
privileges. The KING and his Ministers depend
upon the military skill of Marshal SERRANO,
to whom they and the majority in the Cortes
are ready to give whatever forces he may ask.
Thus far the Republicans in and out of Parlia-
ment 40. ye lent no countenance, direct or in-

direct, to the insurrection. Let King AMADEUS
and his advisors pursue a Wise, moderate, and
patriotic course, and the new order of things
may become settled, and produce happy fruits
for hapless Spain.

articles.title: PATENT LAWS.
articles.text:
THE PATENT LAWS.

Tat: Select Committee on the Patent Laws
have agreed to certain resolutions—which we
publish in another column—which they re-
commend as the basis of legislation on the
subject. They state that the privilege con-
ferred by letters patent promotes the progress
of manufactures by causing many important
inventions to be introduced and developed
more rapidly than would otherwise be the
case; and it does not appear to them that the
granting of pecuniary rewards could be sub-
stituted with advantage to the public interest
for the temporary privilege conferred by letters
patent. At the same time, the existing laws
are defective and require improvement; and
the Committee think that protection for a
limited period, and dating back to the time at
which it was applied for, should only be
granted for an invention on its nature and

particular points Of novelty being clearly
described in a provisional specification, and
upon the report of a competent authority that
such invention, so far as can be ascertained by
such authority, is new, and. is a manufacture
within the meaning of the law. They further
consider that all letters patent should be
subject to the condition that the manufacture
should be carried on within the United King-
dom, and. that it shall be carried into effective
operation within. a reasonable time from the
granting of the patent by, the patentee or his
licencees,

CONDITION OF AGRICULTURAL
LABOURERS IN FRANCE.
[COMMUN WATER.]
TILE position of agricultural labourers is
attracting much attention in France as else-
where, and many remedies are proposed for it
by economists of more or less note. M. EunENE
BOUNEX/ERE, a French writer of some eminence,
has lately contributed to the discussion by
publishing it work in which he pleads the
cause of the Agricultural Commune, and
invites the country labourer to imitate the
town workman in forming associations, in
order thereby to obtain the strength and
knowledge necessary to securing an important
position in society. The revolutions which
have taken place in France during the last
eighty years have produced no serious social
reform. There have been many political
changes, power has passed from this man to
that, but the condition of the labourer and of
women has boon little improved. M. BouNE-
j MERE thinks thinks that, instead of agitating
in favour of ephemeral constitutions the best
practical means of amelioration would be the
establishment of the Commune, "the cellular
element of the great hive in which humanity
works." He shows that the agricultural
labour of Europe was from the earliest ages of
Christianity to the present time carried on by
religious or lay associations. He is one of
those who consider the teaching of CHRIST to
contain a socialistic element, and believes that
the influence of the Christian Church was
democratic and tended towards freedom as
long as it kept close to gospel precepts. The
Communistic principle in Christianity soon
became materially weakened, but communities
of laymen began in the tenth century to carry
on the system which the religious orders had
pursued. They arose from the formation of
colonies round the agricultural establish-
ments of the monks, by the numerous vaga-
bonds and beggars originally attracted thither
by
these colonies,

en con-
siderable towns, took their origin. For .a
long period these labourers remained attached
to soil, and were passed from hand to hand as
property, without themselves acquiring any.
At length they united; and having, by co-
operative labour, increased the produce of the
earth, they obtained possession of it on pay-
ment of certain dues. Hence arose those
societies in Auvergne which haw) benefidial
an effect upon the progress of agriculture, M.

BOUNMERE characteristically attributes their
origin to ,those words in the gospel, "If two
of you shall agree on earth," etc. lie isin
favour of keeping a perfect balance between
the equally legitimate principles of in-
dividuality and association, the free play of
which is needful to social harmony, and dwells
on the advantage of the agricultural associa-
tion of small properties as giving scope to the
use of new processes which each could not
beiar the expense of attempting singly. The
author thinks that in order to organize agri-
cultural communes, the peasants must be
attached to the soil by granting them better
conditions, by attracting the surplus working
populations of the towns into the fields, and
encouraging the creation of industrial agri-
cultural oolonies. " Since," says he, "the
condition of labourers has constantly changed
in the direction of improvement, and that each
of these improvements has marked the hour of
a great and beneficial social transformation,
why should that which has never ceased to
progress be struck motionless? Why should
not the labourer, who has been by turns slave,
serf, and paid workman, be called to the ad-
vantages of association?"
