articles.title: CONSERVATIVE POLICY.
articles.text:
THE CONSERVATIVE POLICY.

Mr. Gathorne Hardy, in concluding a speech
at a- great Conservative banquet held on
Wednesday at Canterbury, said the policy of
the Government had reduced the "groat I
united Liberal Party" to the "great Liberal
Party." It will soon come to the "small
Liberal Party," and, finally, to no party at all.
The right lion, gentleman said that he agreed
with Mr. Laird that the time was approaching
when moderate men would consider it to be
their imperative duty to remain no. longer in
the ranks of the party to which they had
belonged, and he himself longed to see the day
when, in spite of small differences of opinion,
be should find himself united with those who
felt with him upon some of the greatest ques-
tions of the day. It had been said on the
other side that the • Conservatives had no
policy; but this he denied, asserting that
recently it had been defined by statesmen like
Lord Derby and Mr. Disraeli, and was being
exhibited in the House of Lords by the Duke
of Richmond, Lord Salisbury, Lord Carnarvon,
and others, all of whom tided in cordial
unanimity, desirous of advancing the same
interests. What, then, had the Conservative
party to do? The Church was attacked.
It was their duty to defend it—to
take power wherever they could to
advance their interests. When he considered
what the Chureh did, when he knew that
advice and instruction were being administered
in 10,000 parishes in England; when he knew
the consolation that was every day brought to
thousands of homes through the means of
that Church—when he thought of these things,
he trembled to think that there were men so
insane as to deprive themselves of an institu-
tion which did this country so much good.
While giving Mr. Forster credit for the fair-
ness with which he had treated the Conserva-
tives, he still thought more might have been
conceded to the Church party, though, so firm
an Opinion had he of the religious feelings
possessed by Mr. Forster' that he believed he
would never be a party to secular education.
On the • question of endowments, lie main-
tained that the Conservative party must
take their stand and oppose the proposition in
regard to the alteration of their epplica-
tion. Speaking -of - the monarchy, Mr.
Hardy- said they might cast their eyes
abroad, and the lessons taught them would be
all-sufficient. The Conservative party not
only wanted place, but power—power in its
own strength, and not through disunion amOng
its adversaries. After speaking on the question
of our colonies, and advising the maintenance
of intimate relations as opposed to the miser-
able idea of the Government to separate them
front this country on the score of expense, the
gentleman concluded a long speed k by
advising the electors of Kent to seize the
opportunity that would be presented them of
returning to Parliament members holding
heir political views.

articles.title: SUNDAY LABOUR. IN THE POST OFFICE
articles.text:
SUNDAY LABOUR. IN THE POST OFFICE

For some years past the Working Men's
Lord's Day Rest Association has laboured to
obtain Sunday rest for provincial letter carriers
and. rural messengers, and, at their request,
last session Mr. Charles Reed, M.P, for
Hackney, brought the subject under the
notice of the House of Commons, and a
circular has just been issued by the Post Office
Department which provides-
1. That a Sunday rural post shall be taken
off if the receivers of two thirds of the letters
for the district desire its discontinuance.
2. That no Sunday rural post shall be pa
on unless the receivers of two-thirds of tho
letters for the district desire its establish-
ment, or kas the ease may be) its restoration.
The circular also states that rural messengers
who walk 14 miles on week days are to be
relieved by a substitute every, alternate
Sunday at the expense of the Goverment,
and a Sunday delivery in towns may be
abolished at the request of the inhabitants
generally, expressed through the local authori-
ties. All town letter carriers who work :on
Sunday mornings are to be entirely relieved of i
any duty later n the day, and exceptionally
heavy duties on Sunday are to be lightened at
the 'expense of the department. The oolleo-
tions of letters on Sundays, from relieving
offices, and in certain eases from pillar or wall
boxes, is also to be discontinued, so as to con-
find the machinery for posting letters to the
head offices only, and the entire closing, with
certain exceptions, on Sundays of rural post
offices which have no post arrival or dispatch
on that day, IA to be efl'eeted.
Petitions and every information for relieving
the rural messengers from. Sunday deliveries
may be obtained from Mr. Charles Hill,
secretary, Working Men's Lord's Day Rest
Association, 13, Bedford-row, London, W.C.

articles.title: CO-OPERATIVE CONFERENCE AT
articles.text:
CO-OPERATIVE CONFERENCE AT

OLDHAM.

On Saturday afternoon a Co-operative Con-
ference was held at Oldham. There were
about 100 delegates present, and Mr. J. F.
Brearley, Oldham, was called to the chair.
PRODUCTIVE CO-OPERATION.
Mr. W. Nuttall, secretary, read a paper
introducing the first subject, "how best to
extend productive co-operation." He thought
the principle which had succeeded so well in
their retail stores ought to be fully carried out in
their productive stores. The productive stores
should at first manufacture only those articles
which the retail stores required, and these
latter ngaii should act in concert as a market
for the former. The productive stores should
he managed by a committee elected from the
central store, and by a local committee, who
would have a personal knowledge of the
artioles manufactured.

Mr. C. Fitzpatrick (MOssley) thought they
ought to go into the productive department
by a federation of co-operative societies and
individual proprietors. He thought the Man-
chester Wholesale Society had too much work
on their hands successfully to carry out the
proposal.
The Chairman was opposed to the Whole-
sale Society carrying out an amalgamation of
productive stores. He believed that persons
in the localities specially adapted for the pro-
duction of certain articles would. be much
better able to undertake the management of
productive stores than a central committee of
the Wholesale Society.
Mr. Abraham Howard (Rochdale) said he
was opposed to centralisation in co-operation.
If they attempted to carry out that policy they
would soon over-reach themselves. The best
way to succeed, he believed, was by a federa-
tion of societies and of individual effort. That
idea had been suocessfully carried out at

Rochdale and at Oldham.
Mr. Hiton (Manchester) was opposed to Mr.
Nuttall's plan. He wished the area of co-
operation widened, and opportunity given for
more leaders to come to the front. He went
in for individual productive societies, with
proper supervision; in order that the same
amount of diligence might be put forth as their
retail stores have done.
Mr. Benjamin Jones (Blackley) considered
they must have a central depot, with delegates
appointed to see that the productive stores
were managed in a right manner; and the only
way to do that was by uniting the Central
Board with a local government.
Mr. J. Hilton (Middleton) said if every
individual society were to take action there
would be no end of failure. The scheme
could not survive long under mere local ideas;
but they must have one united body, having
the same hopes and interests. He could not
see why the interests of Oldham could not be
as well looked after, and their projects as well
realised, by men managing at Roolidale as
they would be at Oldham itself. (Hear,
hear.)
Messrs. W. Richardson (Oldham), Green-
wood (Hebden Bridge), A.nderton (Failsworth),
Sheppard (Rochdale), and Birehall (Barnsley),
also took part In the discussion, which was
brought to a close by a reply from Mr. Nutt-
all. No resolution was passed.
COTTAGE PROPERTY.

The only other subject discussed was that
of cottage property.
The next conference was appointed to be
held at Manchester.

articles.title: CANON GIRDLE§TONE AND THE
articles.text:
CANON GIRDLE§TONE AND THE

FARMERS.

The name of Canon Girdlestone is well
known as that of a parish priest who has gone
out of his way, to promote what he believed to be
the best interests of the agricultural labourers
in his parish, at the cost of no small amount
of personal odium and ill-feeling. The farmers
and the landlords thought him a meddlesome
fellow, and for a long time he had no friends
who spoke Well of him, save amongst the poor.
He has worked on through this time of dis-
couragement, discharging tho duty ho had
laid upon himself, and gradually raising the
position of the labourer, by opening out to
lam other markets for his labour, and so re-
lieving the burthen of the surplus in his own
locality. In thus acting he has lived to be
bettor understood by those whom he was sup-
posed to be injuring. He has just taken his
farewell of the farmers of Halberton, and was
loudly applauded, we are told, in the advice
he gave to them. He said he should like the
farmers to get the assistance of the legisla-
ture, and obtain some recognition of tenant-
right—a right for farmers to be compensated
for expenses of manure and other -require-
ments for the cultivation of,the soil. It often
pained him, he added, to see men turned out
of their farms without compensation. There
is no doubt that the advice thus given will
yield its fruit hereafter. The question of an
English tenant-right is one of the questions
whuth must come up for legislative action
some time, and recent events have shown that
that time will not be so distant as it promioi
to be a few years ago. The relations between
landlord and tenant in England and Scotland

are happily not of a nature to call for violent
remedies, they are, on the whole, kindly, ho-
nourable, and j ustr—hut occasionally the techni-
cal right of the landlord is so strained until it
becomes a moral wrong, and then we see upon
how slight a tenure the tenant holds his rights,
and how grievous may be the actual injustice
inflicted upon him by the sudden rupture of
this tenure on the mere irresponsible motion
of the landlord. Indeed, we are coming to
recognise the fact, which has already been
recognised in Ireland, that the farmer who
works the land, and. invests his capital in it,
is not merely a tenant, but that lie acquires
other rights which the law in equity should
protect As yet the voice raised in this be-
half is but as the sound of distant murmur-
ings, but that it will become louder.and more
clear no one doubts. We can only hope that
those who may lead the legislature of the das
will be wise enough to listen to it before it
becomes an angry roar.

articles.title: CAT SHOW__AT_THE CRYSTAL
articles.text:
THE CAT SHOW__AT_THE CRYSTAL

PALACE.

This being the third of the Annual Cat
Shows which have been instituted at the Crys•
tal Palace, offers a fair test of the likelihood
there is of similar exhibitions becoming per-
manently popular with the public. Wednes-
day was the open day, and judging by the
number of visitors, and their style and
appearance, we should be very much inclined
to anticipate for the Cat Show a long succes-
sion of successful anniversaries. The cages
or pens are by an improved arrangement
placed lengthways in the north nave, and
their pedestals being much higher than they
were last year, little people and people in the
back rows can got a fair look at the assembled
grimalkins. The entries number 221—N0. 1

being Mr. L. Smith's short-haired tortoise-
shell Tom, value £6O, and No. 204, Mr. W.
C. Fame's Angora, value £lO 10s. Of course
there was a tremendous crowd all day round
pen No. 1 to see what is believed to be the
only genuine tortoise-shell Tom to be found
even in England. The oat was exhibited at
last year's show, and, the Mat he then
obtained has not in the interim produced any
rivals of the pure breed and colour. The price
put on him would hardly, we believe, induce
Mr. Smith to part with his feline Koh-i-noor.
Of the remainder of the show, which includes
Persians, with their long hairy coats,
looking as if ready to be turned at once
into Cashmere shawls; the Angoras,
which although also foreigners, are more
familiar to our oat collectors; the Russians,
cold and slaty, looking like Russia
itself, and the wide varieties of "domestics,"
it may be said that it has been selected with
greater care and a closer view to classification
than that of previous years. The first cat
show, like the first baby show, was a mistake,
the contributors thinking that size would
carry away everything, and consequently the
pens, like the cradles, were filled with un-
shapely, dull-looking monAtrosities. This
year we have colour, " m4ts," figure and
pedigree all carefully attended to, and the
result is a show which, while it pleases the
unskilful, will not make the judicious—that is
to say, the judges—grieve. On the high
authority of Lady Dorothy Nevill and of Me.
Harrison Weir, we can recommend Torb3ise.-
shell No. 1 as combining every,qualifieation
of a oat of high degree, and worth alone a
pilgrimage to Sydenham to "interview."
Judges cannot be prize-seeking exhibitors, or
else the lady whoinsWe have taken the liberty
of quoting, would certainly herself get a prize
for her rare little Siamese cat, so like a pug
dog, and so full of fire and intelligence. 'lle
"domestics" justified their designation by
seeming to be quite at home; the various
foreigners slept or yawned, and such cats as
were .accompanied by their interesting little
kittens played materfamilias with an effusion
that brought tears of sympathy into the eyes
of the lady visitors., We do not know that
there is anything more to be said about
this year's cat show. We may remark, how-
ever, that autumn is considered to be the
best time for holding these shows, as boats
are glossier, and family cares less onerous,
than in the spring of the year.

respecting the treatment of lunatics at the
Asylum at Evero. Several of the officials of

country will be for the first time adequately
appreciated, by the public to-day, when the

Districts which hitherto have been virtually

ana in some eases' notably Cardiff, Llangollen,

lations in France has decided that it is incom-
petent to express an opinion with regard to the
surrender of Paris in aS7I. In the report

M. Jules Favre was invested by the Govern-

siders that it is no part of its duty to pass

M. Glambetta has been presented by, some
Alsaciani with a group of figares in bronze,
illustrating the - attitude of Als:oe towards
France. In thanking thorn for this gift M.
Gambetta said it was not for France to talk of
revenge or to utter rash words, but to give a
pledge to Europe that her only desire is to
attain that position in which, without drawing
the sword, right is recognised "because it is
backed up by strength.'

Advices from Madrid still bring news or the
surrender of the Carlists. Thus 600 are said
to have given themselves up at A.ranaz ; and
one of the insurgent bands, having revolted
against its leaders, has submitted to Brigadier
Rivera. It is ugain announced, too' that the
movement in Navarre is considered, to be at an
end, and telegrams both from Madrid and
from St. Sebastian announce that Marshal
Serrano's forces arc Wing concentrated in
Biscay.

Switzerland—as far as the peopleat large go
—seems to have approved the project of the
revised. , Constitution, which would have the
general effect of substituting a national for a
merely cantonal unity by fusing the whole of
the cantons, for certain purposes, into one.
The numbers were—Ayes, 239,140 ; Noes,
223,023; but, out of 22 cantons, 13 voted
against the revision, and aonsequently the
favourable vote becomes invalid. It is signi-
ficant that all the Roman Catholic cantons
were against the revision.

Viscount Parker, late an officer in the
Grenadier Guards, and heir to the earldom of
Macclesfield, having been adjudicated a bank-
rupt some months since, failed to appear at
the sittings of the court. Ho is resident at
New York; and application was Made to
examine him there under a COMIIII3BiOII to be
granted by the Court. The Hon. W. C.
Spring-ltioo, though characterising:the appli-
cation as a novel one, gave permission for the
trustee to make the examination in such mode
aa he might be advised,.

At the Mansion-house police-court on Mon-
day a woman named Graham, 33 years of age,
was sentenced to three months' imprisonment
with hard labour, for having obtained money
.by false pretences from Mr. Swanston, a City
merchant. At Marlborough-street, a young
gentleman named Remington was charged
With obtaining £1,450 by fraud from a Mr.
Bernard Engel, and the prosecutor having been
examined, an adjournment took place, the
defendant being released on his own recog-
.nizanee. At Southwark, a case was heard in
which a young woman was committed to prison
in default of finding sureties for her good
behaviour towards one of the witnesses against
the two women, Murray and Lynch, and whom
she had threatened with violence for giving
evidence against them at the trial which
ended in their being sentenced to penal servi-
tude for life.

A case of brutality on the part of a constable
was before the magistrate at Clerkenwell
Police-court on Monday. Some difficulty
having been experienced in taking an intoxi-
cated drover to the station-house, the police-
man in whose custody he was struck him on
the head and broke the man's skull. The
drover, who had been arrested for drunkenness,
was discharged, Mr. Cooke expressing au
opinion that the constable had used a great
deal of unnecessary violence, and that his con-
duct ought to be brought before the Chief
Commissioner.

Mallow, the representation of which ig
vacant through the appointment of Mr. Waters,
Q.C., to a county ohturmanship, is one of
.the
smallest borough constituencies in the United
Kingdom. There are not more than 200 deg
,-
tors upon the register, and at the last three
contests the number of 'voters who have gone
to the poll wore 130, 103, and 123 respec-
tively. Tho struggle which appeared to excite
less interest than any since the passing of the
first Reform Act was in 1850, when Mr. Robert
Longfield polled 68 votes:against 55 recorded
for Sir Japhson Norreys. The present Master
of the Rolls in Ireland, the Right Hon. Edward
Sullivan, was the predecessor of Mr. Waters
in the representation of this borough.

According to a Washington telegram a com-
promise is likely to be arrived at between
Great Britain and the :United States on the
subject of the Indirect Claims by a supple-
mentary treaty which will release both countries
from liability for indirect damages. A .New
York Correspondent, writing on the 30th tilt.,
says that Mr. Fish has always been ready to
surrender the Indirect Claims, but that the
real obstacle to a settlement has been Presi-
dent Grant. In taking up this position, how-
ever, the President has met with anything but
support from the country. The tone and lan-
guage of Mr. Bancroft Davis's Case have been,
universally condemned, and the expressions of
regret that worthless and irritating claims
should have been set fortk in a needlessly
offensive manner have been general and de.
aided. Mr. Fish's proposal of an agreement
between the two countries stipulating that a
neutral shall never be held responsible except
for the diroot consequences of a broach of
neutrality, is likely, to be cordially accepted
by the country if it results in a settlement of
the dispute, but it will injure tho President
and the Secretary of State peronally—not
because they have yielded, but because they
took up a position they were unable to
maintain.

A fatal yachting accident occurred on the
Thames oti: Grays on Saturday afternoon. The
chip was fixed for the opening sail of the
Junior Thames Yacht Club (Greenbithe), and
one of the members, a gentlemaa named
Tracey, living at Dartford, and the owner of a
small yacht called the Minnie, was cruising
about before coming up to the. stition, but
when off Grays the yacht was caught in a
violent squall and blown over, the three oceu-
pants being thrown into . the -water. Mr.
Tracey only was drowned, the two othety
being picked up by a. boat s(nt to their assist-
ance. The yacht filled and 34.ak almost im-
mediately.

The Empress of Germany embarked from
Dover on luesday morning, having been ac-
companied from London to that town by Prince
Arthur.

At a meeting of the Commission of Sawers
it was reported that during the past fortnight
4,333 lbs. of meat had been seized in tile
markets and slaughter-houses of the City, and
destroyed as unlit for humah food.

A large and influential meeting was held at
Willis's Rooms on Tuesday, in aid othe Siwcial
Endowment Fund of King's College. The
Archbishop of Canterbury presided, and Mr.
Gladstone, the Bishop of Peterborough, and
Mr. W. 11. Smith, M.P., were amongst the
speakers. Resolutions were passed declaring
that King's College deserved the conhdenee
and support of all who accepted religion as
the basis of true education, and that the pre-
sent effort to clear 'off the debt and form . the
nucleus of a moderate endowment was wen-
, tial to the welfare, of the institution*:

011 Tuesday evening her Majesty, accom-
panied by Prince Leopold and Princess
Beatrioe, left Windsor Castle for Balmoral.

--
There was a prosecution at the Lambeth
Police-court on Tuesdor for the sale of un-
wholesome meat, and for this offence a trades-
man Was tined V, with the alternative of a
months' imprisonment.

It is announced from Paris that Marshal
Ilazainc surrendered himself into custody on
Tuesday morning, to await his trial by court-
martial.

A woman named Cullum, 26 years of age,
has been committed for trial from the Clerken-
well police-court on a charge of having stolen
a little boy nearly four years old. At the
same court a man was brought up for cruelly
treating his children, and in default of finding
sureties for his good behaviour, was sent to
prison. At Southwark, Julia Mills, a servant,
20 years of age, was remanded on a chrirKe of
abandoning her child, one year and nine
months old, in one of the alleys of Bermondsey.

Last week the aggregate mortality in Lon-
don and 20 other large towns of the United
Kingdom was at the rate of 23 deaths annually
to every 1,000 persons estimated to be living.
In the metropolis 2,123 births and 1,250
deaths were registered, the former having
been 164 and the latter 227 below the average.
Thirty-nine persons died from small-pOx, 3.5.
from measles, 10 from scarlet fever, 9 from
diphtheria, 83 from whooping-cough, 27 from
different forms of fever (of which 4 were
certified as typhus, 15 as enteric or typhoid)
and 8 as simple continued fever), and 10 from
diarrhoaa. The mean temperature was Only
47.2 degs., and 4 2 degs. below the average
for the corresponding week in fifty years; the
mean on Sunday, sth, was 51.9 degs., and

diseases of the respiratory organs, including
phtbisis, Ircr: 317.

From April Ist to the 11th inntant the Ex-
chequer receipts amounted to £8,337,770, as
compared with £6,938,070 in the correspond-
ing period of last year. The expenditure has
been p 9,298,309. The balance in the Bank

The Registrar in Bankruptcy has made an
order enabling the trustee of Viscount Parker's
estate to proceed to America, for the purpose
of examining the bankrupt, who lately failed
for £25,000.

That which is known as the betting nuisance
in Knightsbridge was the subject of proceed-
ings on Tuesday against four men, who wore
described as commission agents, and charged
with obstructing a public: thoroughfare.
Betting-books were found upon all the defend-
ants at the time of their arrest. Each of them
was fined L 5.

The President of the Oxford University
Boat Club has announced that in anticipation
of the Atalanta crew putting in an appearance
at Ilealey.on-Thamas Regati a, a presentation
prize, value 25 guineas, with medals, will be
offered for competition by crews in four-oared
boats without coxswains. It is anticipated
that both Universities will be represented on
the occasion.

General Sir James Chatterton, Bart., K.C.B ,
is fast recovering from his long and serious
indisposition, Sir Wiliianj Gull, Bart., Sir
James Paget, Bart., and Sir William Jeuner,
Bart., have been in constant attendance on the
gallant oflioer.

At an important meeting of shareholders
of the Metropolitan Railway Company, a
question largely affecting the interests of the
community was mooted. Mr. B. Grant, who
was appointed chairman of the committee of
shareholders, after regrettink the frequent
want of unity between themselves and the
directors, adverted to the too patent fact that
those who travel short journeys have to .pay
as much as those whO go long distances. lie
recommended the appointment, of some com-
petent financial firm to deal with the question
of accourits. A matter of less general interest,
viz., the retention of waste lands by the com-
pany in anticipation of 'a rise in value, was
also deal with. An amendment, however,
was careed to the effect that it was inexpe-
dient that any action should be taken until
the general body of shareholders had received
a report from those directors specially ftp-
rinted to watch their interests.

Amid the warlike intelligence that has for
so long a time formed the staple of Spanish
news, it is an agreeable change to read that a
meeting was held in Madrid for the purpose of
considering a proposal t 5 hold a Univeml
Exhibition there in 1873.

In the French Budget or 1873 there is
an estimated deficit of 120 millions Of frornoF,
which the Goverment proposes to cover by- a
tELK on raw materials. .

The United Kingdom Band of Hope Union
hold its seventeenth annual meeting on Tues-
day night at Exetdr-hall.

His Royal Highness the Field-Marshal
Commanding-in-Chief , has approved of the
troops at the camp being formed into four
divisions for drill purposes and with a view to
their . organisation- for the forthcoming
Autumn Maneettvres. The cavalry division
will be commanded by Major-General Sir
Thorns! M‘Mahon, 0.11 ; the first infantry
division will be under Major-General Lysons
C:B., and the second under Major-General
Smith, C.B , and the third under Major-
General Maxwell. A battery of Artillery, a
Company of Engineers, and a section of the
Engineer Train will be attached to each divi-
sion. Colonels Seymour, C. 1., 2nd Dragoon
Guards; Weare, C. 8., 50th Regiment; Watson
82nd Regiment; Anderson, 22nd ; Brice, 17th;
Catty, 46th; and Spurgin, C. 13 , C. 5.1., 102nd
Regiments, will command brigades.

Tier Majesty will, it is expected, remain in
the Highlands for about five weeks, and will
then return to Windsof. Prince Leopold, who
accompanies her Majesty, is. sufbring from a
sprained ankle, and, on leaving Windsor, had
to be carried from the waggonette to the train.

Robert Francis, tlecond Baron Gifford, died
at his residence, Ampney Park, near Ciren-
cester, on Monday night, after a long illness.
He is succeeded by his oldest son, Ldric
Frederick, who is a lieutenant in the 83rd
Foot.

Dr. Pnsey is sufficiently recovered from his
late indisposition to be able to mum his duties
at Oxford. He is announced as one of the
University preachers at St. Mary's on Sunday
next, when he will preach " On the -Jewish
Interpretation of Prophecy."

Eighteen mere French Communiz-ts were
lan dud at Dover on Tuesday, by the mail paeket
from Calais, on their way to London. They
had all been recently released from custody,
and appeared to have been expatriated in a
rather destitute state.

The Bishop of Chester has collated the Rev.
Charles Bowen, M.A., Rector of St, Mary's-
with-Upton, and Chaplain to the Garrison,
Chester, to an honorary canonry in Chester
Cathedral,

It is proposed to form a National Associa-
tion on the question of the Income Tax, for
the purpose of abolishing Schedule D. In aid
of this projeot, a conference, composed of' re-
presentatives of commercial and political asso-
ciations and private speakers, will be held on
Wednesday and Thursday, the 22nd and 23rd
instant, at Birmingham, under the auspices
of the Birmingham Anti-Ineome-Tax Asso-
ciation. Several members of Parliament have
been invited to attend.

Mr. Price and Mr. Monk, the Liberal mem-
bers for Gloucester, met tkeir constituents on
Tuesday evening, and received a vote of
confidence. Mr. Price expressed his belief
that when the cloud which now darkened the
political horizon had blown away, Mr. Glad-
stone and his Cabinet would be as popular as
ever, and even now, if the Conservatives
assumed the reins of Government, the Liberal
party would again, and that immediately, be
firmly united.

The Liberal members for Cambridge, Mr.
R. Torrens and Mr. W. Fowler, addressed
their constituents on Tuesday evening. Mr.
Torrens expressed his entire sympathy with
the agricutural labourers' movement. Mr.
Fowler condemned the interference of work-
men on strike'vvith those who chose to work.,
and expressed his conviction that the Govern-
ment would come scatheless out of the
American question. Both speakers said they
would not vote for thd Ballot Bill when
returned from the Lord's if secret voting was
not left compulsory. A unanimous vote of
confidence was passed in favour of both
members.

The Rectory of Hertingtordbury, near Hert-
ford, has become, vacant by the death of the
Rev. W. Gill, M.A. It is worth £5OO a year,
and is in the gift of the Chancellor of the
Duchy of Lancaster. The Rectory of Lang-
ford, near Maldon Essex, has become vacant
by the death of die Rev. C. V. Shuekbarght
It is worth £2OO a year, and is in the gift of
the Hon. F. Byron.

According to the Scotsman, a document,
signed by 516 electors and non•eleetors of the
Border. Burghs, has been forwarded to Mr.
Trevelyan,,M.P,, protesting against the course
he has taken up in regard to the Permissive
Bill, and declaring that had he expressed him-
self asi3trongly at eleetion time he would not
have been returned„ Mr. Trevelyan has re-
plied that at that time other questions were
more before the public, and that, his subsequent
conduct has not been inconsistent with his
past declarations. A rejoinder informs Mr.
Trevelyan that his Leply is not satisfactory.

The
.manufacture of torpedoes is just- now
going on briskly in the Royal Laboratory at
Woolwich and already several thousands of
the ordinary class are stored ready for use at a
moment's notice. These aro for placing in
harbours, for the purpose of preventing the
entry of ships, and they are arrange.l to be
fired by electricity from the shore. Another
kind of torpedo has, however, been designed
for agressive purposes. It is made in
the shape of a fish, is some five feet in length,
and has a tail which works as a screw pro-
peller. It can be sent with almost uuerring
aim against the sides of a ship four hundred
yards distant, and would, of course, be very
destructive in its operations: Other kinds of
submarine artillery are in construction; but
their description is a profound secret, only
trusty. men being employed in making them,
and the work being performed at night, in a
portion of the Laboratory set apart for that
purpose.

The agitation for increased Wages and shorter
hours of labour prevalent throughout the
country at present has manifested itself
amongst the metropolitan police who complain
of insufficient pay .and overwork. Some time
ago the inspectors and sergeants obtained an
increase Of salary, but the common constables
have continued at the old rates; and it is
alleged a number of the old members of the
foi Oa, wile, by length of seivice are entitled to
superannuation, are constantly applying for
d:s large unless the grievances complained of
are to be immediately redressed. The fact
that. the Secretary of State has recently ap-
proved of an advanced scale of payumit for
the Lancashire police, who receive on joining
2.,;. 9'l. weekly, gradually atigwenting•to
..Vl. 63. 101., with pensions, gratuities, and
reasonable periods of vacation, has increased
the dissatisfaction of the metropolit m force
with their present position and pros,Rots..

On Wednesday evening Count Beust,lthe
Austro llungariau Ambassador, presided• at
the anniversary dinner of the Society of
Friends and Foreigners in distress. A dona-
tion of A;100 was announced from her Majesty,
and it was stated that the Emperor of Austria
bad raised his subscription from £3O to £lOO
per annum.

The Irish Home Government Assee'ation
have just held a meeting in Dublin. Mr. P.
J. Smyth, M.P., presided, and Mr. Redmond,
M.P., and Mr. John Martin, M.P., were also
amongAt the speakers. A. letter was read from
Dean O'Brien, declaring that his sympathy
with the national movement had not lessened
or changed.

Viscount Milton, M.P. for the southern
division of the West Riding, having left
England for tho benefit of his health, the
West Riding Liberal Association has resolved
to request his lordship not to resign his seat.

A shipping agent was charged at the Man-
sion House with unlawfufully unship lug a
largo quantity of cigars and tobacco, under
pretence that they were for exportation to
Calcutta, in which ease duty would not be
charged; he conveyed them to his own shop
and to that of an( t er t)baoconist. The case
was remanded until Friday; hail to the extoit
of £4OO being accepted for the prisener's re-
appearance. -

There appears to be some uncertainty with
regard to the returns of the Swiss plobiseitum;
but, as already announced, the number of the
Cantons in favour of the revision Of the Con-
stitution was only nine' there being thirteen
opposed. The Federal Assembly is to meet
on the 27th inst., just to be made acquainted
with the results of the voting.

According to the Poor-law Returns, the
total number of paupers last week in the
metropolis was 110,01,3, of whom 33,074 were
in workhouses, and 76,941 received oat-door
relief. Compared with the corresponding
week in 1871, 1870, and 1869, these figures
show a decrease of 19,908, 30,500, and 26,471
respectively. The number of vagrants relieved
was 906.

At the Aldershot Petty Sessions, last week,
Captain Neweome (chairman), G. F. 13irch,
Esq. and Captain Elliott being on the bench,
an old man of sixty, named John Cranham,
was charged with stealing a few chips, of the
alleged value of twopence, the property of
Messrs. rook, builders. According to the
Alderdiat Gazette the ease was one of a most
trivial character. The prisoner alleged That
ho picked up the chips on a footpath, and
notwithstanding the fact that he bore a
twenty years' good character, and lutd been in
prison for four or live days since his appre-
hension, the magistrates, to the great surprise
of all in court, sentenced him to undergo
three weeks' imprisonment with bard labour,
saying they must make an example of such
eases. A sad scene was witnessed outside the
court. The wife and son of the unfortunate
man were weeping in an hysterical manner,
and lamenting, to use their own words, that
" they should have been robbed of their good
name."

—Speculation in Washington is very active as
to the fate of the proposed new Article of the

yesterday. A majority oethe 'Senate approve

corresponding member of the section of Po.

Wesleyan minister, has been preaching at

at- the office of the Illustrated London News

his foot, when ho slipped, and was dragged
round. A few minutes elapsed before he could
be extricated. lre was taken to King's-College

The Bank of Paris, in conjunction with its

Detective Briden, of the K Division, has

March 15th. The prisoner is Charles Davis,
aged. 23, picture-frame maker, of Leman-
street, I.undon, and has been consigned to
Dart ford Police-station. He was arrested at

the King's Arms Inn, Mile-end-road, whilst
assisting at a benefit for the defence of the
parties now lying in 'Maidstone Gaol awaiting
their trial for manslaughter.
Her Majesty arrived at Balmoral on Wed-
nesday. As the train stopped at Ferry-hill
on Wednesd.ay morning her Majesty received
a hearty welcome from a largo assemblage.
Balloter was reached at twenty-five minutes
past two in the afternoon. Prince Leopold was

Mr. John Bright left Perth on IVedneBday
morning by the Highland railway train at
11.50 a.m. for Dalguise; Blair Atli°le.

The Galway election inquiry was resumed
yesterday, when the council for the sitting
member continued his address. Judge Keogh
is expected to give his decision on Monday
next.

Mr. Horace Greeley has retired from the
management of the New York Tribune during
the Presidential canvas.
At the Westminster Police-court, on Wed•
nesday, the Marquis Townshend appeared to
prosecute a cabmen for cruelty to his horse.
As, however, the man had expressed his re-

A Paris Correspondent says that disastrous

the crops by the severe weather whieh has

of the market gardens near the French capital
have particularly suffered, and the same
the case with the vines in the south. In

Mr. Edward Brooke, citizen and clock-
maker, has been nominated one of the Sheriffs
of London for the ensuin,,;t'year.. His colleague
will probably be Mr. Alderman White, who
stands next in rotation amongst the City
magistrates for the office.
Cord Shaftesbury, in presiding over the an-
nual meeting. Of the National: Refuges for

of4the usefulness of this organisation in rescu-

In the Court of Queen's Bench, on Wedues,
dav, an action was brought to recover compen-

'The plaintiff was about 2,5 or 26 years of age,
and the daughter of an inkmaker residing in

,jury
awarded the plaintiff £3OO. A similar aetiOu

A FREE DINNER TABLE,
To the Editor of the Beu-llive.
Sin,—The re-publication of the annexed
extract from "The People's Blue Book," by
by Charles Tennant, may
.perhaps just now be
well timed as a recommendation to the mem-
bers of unions of agricultural labourers to
agitate for a "Free Dinner Table" by the
removal of all taxation from beer drank any-
where except in public homes. Beer taken
with meals is wholsome and nourishing, and
if ordinarily used in this way, tippling in
public-houses would _seldom be resorted to,
and drunkenness would become an excep-
tional vice.
Beer his got such a bad name by its abuse
that men are afraid to plead for its general
use, but the distinction between beer drank
with food, and tippling in an ale-house is so,
clear that nothing but inveterate prejudice
can confound them.
Moreover cheap beer would be good heer
, cheapness and competition would put an end
to adulteration. Charles Tennant, in "The
People's Blue Book," says : •
"In 1745, the farm labourer bought hie
barley at 28. 3d. per bushel, turned it into
malt, paid no tax—(the cottagers were not
then taxed)—and made excellent ale for his,
own use at ad. per quart. Beer, best adapted
to support outdoor labour, is now kept from
the people, being made, by legislation, too
dear for them. An infusion of a plant brought
from China is made cheaper to the working
man than an infusion of a plant grown by the
cottage door. The home barley grower is in-
jured for the benefit of the Chinese tea
grower, and all our working men are injured
morally and physically to an extent beyond
human calculation. This is British Legisla-
tion. Tea is very good for quenching thirst,
but, when exclusively used, requires a full
diet, and, when that cannot be obtained, there
is the desire for some potent stimulant. Hence
the Chinese find the necessity for opium; and
English, Scotch, and Irish labourers who
drink tea and are too poor to bay sufficient
food, resort to gin and whisky. The love of
strong drinks is not natural to the English,
but is created by the English law. William
111. and Queen Anne taxed malt, and made
the beer too dear for the people, and en-
couraged the extraction of spirits from barley
for the sake of revenue. Thus, the British
Legislature created artificially the taste for
strong drinks.
"If good, wholesome beer were allowed to be
brewed in the cottage, or to be bought at a
price at which the labourer and his family
could obtain it, this would supply food and
diminish drunkenness. The rich man, with
abundance of wine and spirits in his cellar, is
seldom tipsy. He has no reason for drinking
to excess. He can always have it, and learns
from experience the value of moderation. The
labouring man, in the like position, would act
in the same way. It is the forced abstinence
in the previous days of the week causes the
abuse on Saturday. But beer, free from
adulteration, can now scarcely be had, for
money. The exhausted labourer drinks, and
by drinking salt and worse ingredients, be-
comes more thirsty. He is doubly robbed—
robbed in character because he drinks too
much—robbed in pocket because he is cheated.
He is then driven to gin, and dies a drunkard,
or is hanged as a murderer. For all this the
British Legislature is responsible."—Yours,

AN AMERICAN ON TRADES' UNIONS.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

-h-a—vo—littely read in the BEE-HIVE
an admirable speech of Mr. G. Potter, defend-
ing trades unions from the charges of a Mr.
Newmarch, and in another number of the
BEE•IIIVE an excellent paper by Mr. Daniel
Guile.

I cannot tell you how intensely I feel that
trades unions are the very root and founda-

tion of the labour movement, and 6 ,
near approach of the coming- struggle (too
vast ear too momentodk.- US; bte spoken- of
hastil3i);`You ought to* d'Otible—ana treble your
exertions to make that foundation as strong, as
self-reliant, as intelligent, and as humane as
possible. There is not a day to be
lost. One thing let me tell you in confi-
dence, as it wonld not be wise to state it
publicly in England—America will prove a
drag to the labour movement. The fact that
all, men, however ignorant, have a vote, makes
them the dupes of politicians and gives igno,
ranee too much the upper hand. Thus the
social and political phases of the labour move-
ment clash with each other. The men look
too much to legislation and too little to bull?
vidual self-reliance and combined social action
to remedy their grievances.
Now, to check this, redouble your egorta in
Great Britain and leave not a stone un-
turned to conciliate Ireland and to unite Irish
with English working men. Next send half-
a-dozen of the ablest leaders of the British
working people over here, and let them
address the American people in the cities and
towns throughout the States. Then let them
take measures with the best trades unionists
here, and organise a universal scheme of
trades unionism and co-operatiol on an
American basis. If I mistake not, President
Grant will soon turn out to be the worst enemy
to the working people.
New, what is to be done to lift trades unions
to a higher level, and to extend industrial
partnerships and co-operation. The first thing
is to stop working overtime, and to devote one
hour gained to sound education. Means must
be taken to increase the circulation of the
BEE-HIVE, and have the gist of its contents
read and explained every week to meetings of
the working people. This should be done by
intelligent working men. Every penny spent
now in this will, in course of time, produce
thousands of pounds worth of good.
Now, how may the surplus funds of trades'
societies be best utilised for the benefit of the
whole nation. Let each trade society devote
ten per cent. of its surplus funds for promoting
the associative production of those articles
most needed by the working people, and five
per cent, of its surplus funds towards the next
strike for eight hours.
Then, with a liberal capital, establish a
scheme of associative production on the eight
hours' basis, and, in order to render it a suc-
cess select the best workmen and let it be
managed by a good business man, acquainted
with that branch of manufacture, In this way
the best articles could be sold at a fraction
less than the current rates, and so command
the market, for of course, the best workmen,
working for themselves and. their fellow-
workmen in associative production could
manufacture a better article at less
cost than inferior workmen.

A portion of the profits, should then be ap-
plied towards paying off the loan of the other
trade societies, and another portion be put
into a fund to promote the labour movement.
in the interest of the whole of humanity. I
know how easy it is to write and how difficult
to carry out these schemes, but if I make one
new practical suggestion it may not be in
vain. Should the plan succeed, enlarge the
business, increase the number of men and give
them a share of the profits.
My idea is to establish one thoroughly good
and successful example of associative prod.uo-
tion so as to gradually convert existing trades
unionism into one grand scheme of associative
production. Then we could build co-operative
ships, man them with co-operative crew's,
who would supply the people on the principle
of " cost the limit of price.'
I write as earnestly as if I were praying, for
I feel somehow or other Great Britain is to be
largely the salvation of America. Go on and
prosper in the good work. "Put God in your
debt, every stroke shall be repaid."—Yours
very sincerely,
Boston, United States.

GEORGE WALKER.
